A long time. But we have a system by which we use the oldest manufactured and keep the newest, so there is none of it kept a very long time.
Then he refers to the increase in the engineering service and the maintenance of military property. Well, we are getting more rifle ranges, and military properties and camp grounds; and of course these have to be maintained. There was no engineering staff twelve years ago, there were no engineers.
Do your engineers take charge of the armouries?

No. The armouries are in charge now of enlisted men, as a rule, of soldiers who have to pass a certain examination to qualify them for taking charge of rifles and equipment of all kinds, and in the case of artillery, men thoroughly conversant with guns and ordinance.

What buildings do your
engineers have charge of?

That refers to the engineering service which controls all the construction and repairs of buildings. When a building is completed, like an armoury, which is done by the Public Works Department, it is handed over to our department, and I think it is under the control of the Quarter-Master General.
For instance, the cottages you built at.Kingston, were the plans prepared by your engineers?

Yes. In that case of course the work is done by the Public Works Department. The engineering branch of the Militia Department prepares plans, and these plans are sent to the Public Works Department. I have endeavoured to establish a joint committee of the two departments, an inter-departmental committee, and thought I had succeeded; but unfortunately, I do not know whose fault it is, the officers committee was interrupted, and they are not meeting at present. I hope to be able to re-establish 72
that committee. If that could be done, and a meeting held once a month or once a fortnight of two or three of the leading
officers of the two departments, it seems to me a good many things which have happened-I am not referring to anything in particular-but the clashing of the two departments would be avoided. There has not been as good results from the working together of the two departments as there ought to have been, and as I would like to see.
Now one of the increases in the militia estimates most criticised in certain quarters is that for the headquarters and district staff. I will not detain the committee by reading the memorandum on these various points, because it is in the hands of the members of the committee, and they will have an opportunity of reading it at their leisure.
In connection with paragraph 52, does the hon. minister mean to say that if war actually took place, he is able now to call out 90,000 men and equip and feed them at a moment's notice?

That subject is fully dealt with. It would not be possible perhaps to-morrow to do that, but it is expected to be able to do it within the very near future. For instance, we have not enough rifles in the country to-day. One does not care to make these admissions, but as a matter of fact there is not at the moment sufficient, but soon will be. The artillery is not anything like the strength it should be, but still is efficient as far as it goes, and steady improvement in all these respects is taking place. As I have already said, I would commend this memorandum to the careful consideration of every hon. member of this committee who is interested in this question.
Now, the question may be asked: Is this system that we are pursuing the wisest and the best? As I have already said, it is a system that has been evolved by experience. We have not changed suddenly-it has been against our policy to do so-the conditions which I found in existence in 1896. We have had the good fortune to have with us during several yeaTS of my regime one of the ablest officers in the British army. I refer to General Sir Percy Lake. I found him here when I came into office. He had been here, I think, two or three years under the late administration. He remained until his term of five years' service was completed, when he went back to his regiment and served in India, and then was brought to the War Office where he performed distinguished service during the war in South Africa. He came here again, four or five years 8-go, to take the position of chief of the general staff. He is absolutely familiar with the working and development of the militia in Canada for the last fifteen or six-



teen years, and, whatever credit is to be given for the position which the militia has attained to-day as a well organized and efficient force is more due to General Sir Percy Lake than to any one else. I cheerfully accord to him the justice of making that statement.
I was saying that we have not introduced any abrupt changes, that we have rather taken the course of building up that which existed, which, I think, is the sound course to pursue. I believe that Jhe_ results ha,ve been good in the main. I believe that, in the main, the country has got the full value of the very considerable amount of money it has spent. When you come to think of it, after all, we are spending less than $1 per head of the population. In the United States they spend $3 or $4 per head of the population, even without taking account of the enormous pensions. If you go to Europe, you find that even the mother country spends $7 or $8 per head.
I believe it is possible to carry on the development and maintenance of the militia with very little increase over the amount that is now being expended. If the estimates of the current year-there have been considerable reductions for the year 1909-10 -could be maintained (and that is less than $1 per head of the population), I should be inclined to think that would be sufficient, at any rate for the present needs, and perhaps for a long time to come. And, when I speak of $1 per head of the population, I do not mean that the expenditure should in-crease_ as the population increases. I do not think that will be necessary. Some additional expenditure will be necessary of course. You cannot increase the strength of the militia without increasing the money you spend. If you send 60,000 men into camp it will cost you twice as much-or nearly so-as if you sent 30,000. You have to feed and clothe and transport these men. Then, we have the great northwest country in which the militia has scarcely been developed at all. _ A few years ago, the question of defending that great country was scarcely considered. The conditions have changed entirely in ten years, and whoever has to administer the militia of Canada during the next ten years will have to consider very carefully the question of putting the militia of the west on the same basis as the militia of the east.
Now, I would like to draw the attention of the committee to the financial side of this question. I do not mean the amount of money being expended, for I have discussed that to some extent and will not deal with it further until we come to the items of the estimates. I desire to discuss the question of how the money is dealt with, _ which is an extremely important question, and one which, very properly, has engaged the attention of public men and of the people for some time past.

Are due precautions taken and safeguards provided for the expenditure of this money? Is due forethought taken in framing estimates as a basis of this expense? I believe it is. At any rate, the course pursued is something like this:	The officers in the
districts and at headquarters who are responsible for carrying on the various services of the militia, are required at a certain period of the year, to send in to headquarters a statement of their requirements for the next year. These requirements are carefully scanned by the officer in charge of the particular branch interested. Eventually, these estimates are brought together and are considered by the deputy minister and by _ the minister, and usually they are considered in very considerable detail by the minister, with the assistance of the members of the Militia Council. We cannot know, of course, what the Finance Minister's position may be. It is difficult to get a statement in advance- perhaps six months before the estimates are made up-of how much money will be available. So, the estimates are made up and are sent to the Finance Minister, under the signature of the Minister of Militia, and, after due consideration-as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) would know-and after queries and so on, it is decided whether these estimates can go through as they have been sent in, or will have to be sent back. It is no breach of confidence to say, with regard to our present estimates, that the estimates which we sent in were not accepted, and that we had a good deal of difficulty in trv-mg to reduce them at rather short notice. It may be that some of our estimates may not come out as we had hoped or expected, but there will not be any very great divergence. Well, what happens next? The money is voted to the different departments, and requisitions are made out, coming chiefly through the Quartermaster General, who has charge of all the stores, and the Master General of Ordnance, who is responsible for the arming of the militia and these in turn are sent to the deputy minister, by whom they are brought to me, and then, if they are approved, they are handed over to the Director of Contracts; because we have in the Department of Militia, and have had for a considerable time, a purchasing branch under the control of that officer. The Director of Contracts then proceeds upon certain lines to ask for tenders. With regard to all the provisions and supplies for the camps and for the permanent force, including fuel and forage, tenders are invariably asked by public advertisement or by public notice posted up.
In your department do you make a discrimination in this advertising between Liberal and Liberal-Conservative newspapers ?

The price is fixed by the Printing Bureau, and the name of the paper, I am told by the deputy- which shows how little notice I have taken of that-is supplied by the department. So far as we can possibly keep down the expense of advertising in the newspapers, we do it. When I came into the department,
I found that for all the camps and for most of the depots, the supplies were asked for by posters posted up in post offices and other public places. A year ago or so some exception was taken to that. It was alleged that the posters were not put up; somebody who wanted to tender said that he had not seen the notice. Therefore we tried advertising in one or two newspapers in each town, in addition to the posters; and we have come to the conclusion that the money spent in advertising in the newspapers is wasted, as we get no more tenders, and that the old system of posters is really sufficient and probably the best. But I have not answered the question. I think it is more than probable that the ordinary course would be to advertise, for instance, in the city of Toronto, in the ' Globe,' and perhaps in the ' Star.' I do not think the ' advertisement would be sent either to the ' Mail and Empire ' or to the ' News '; but I do not think I would go the length of sending an advertisement to an obscure newspaper because it happened to be on my own side of politics.
I have had the Director of Contracts supply me with a memorandum as to the course pursued by him. I have asked him to ascertain the course followed by the War Office and the Admiralty in England, and I will read a few extracts:
Here is an extract from the report of an investigation that took place in England into the letting of contracts during the South African war:
Q. When you receive those requisitions for the purchase of supplies you issued advertisements to the trade?-A. We issued tenders to the trade as a general rule. There is an annual advertisement issued to the trade in order to invite people to come in for competition, and certain requirements are specially advertised from time to time, but as a general rule we issue tenders only to those people who are on our list.
In that connection I want to say that I caused a very careful examination to be made of several English newspapers, including the London 'Times', for a great many years back, and I failed to find one advertisement for any stores, except this kind of an advertisement, which appeared in the London ' Times ' :
Annual notice of army contracts. Notice is hereby given that tenders for specified quantities of the undermentioned articles of manufacture are invited from time to time as required.
Then there is a long list beginning with 'A' and ending with *W'.
72i
Manufacturers who may wish to be invited to tender for army requirements should state the particular articles which they manufacture and the names of at least two well-known firms or publio body who have purchased from them and are in a position to certify as to the quality of their production. The services of an intermediary are unnecessary in approaching the department for this purpose. No ap-lication is neoessary from firms whose names are already on the War Office list. All applications should be in writing and addressed to the Secretary, War Office, London.
From which it appears that the invariable practice of the War Office and Admiralty is to1 issue forms of tenders to people selected who are on the list and not to ask in a general way for tenders for a specific thing.
That is done every year in England. They begin by inviting tenders for all the supplies and every one is given an opportunity to tender.

Not at all, my hon. friend did not catch the point. An advertisement is put in the 'Times' informing those interested that contracts will be let and asking any one who wishes to be put on the list to make application, and he will be put on, provided he can show that he has ever done any work, and gives the names of people who can certify that he is fit to be put on. If he does this, his name will be put on the list, and then forms of tenders will be sent to him.
Is that what is done in your department?

While that has not been done, I have been considering seriously the advisability of doing it. I have only been studying this branch of the subject within a short time and was not fully aware of the course pursued. But I think it is a very desirable course and would save the department an immense amount of trouble. We have a list in the department.
Will the hon. gentleman have any objections to giving us that list?
I have not got it here but I do not think there would be any objection.
Would the minister lay that list on the table?
I have not the list here.
You could bring it tomorrow.
I would have to consider that. I am trying to make this statement absolutely free from any political or party bias whatever. I know that my hon. friend is greatly surprised and disappointed.
No, it does not cost anything to make a statement.

I am not in the habit of making a statement unless it is correct. I was about to say that my instructions to the director of contracts are that whenever a name is put on our list, he shall take pains to consult the commercial agencies or banks or in other ways, to get information as to the character of that particular firm. And unless the evidence is sufficient to show that that firm is entitled to confidence, it will not remain on the list. These are the instructions given, and I think they are followed. As to the politics of the firm, which are on the list. I have not made special inquiries. I happen to know that some of the largest contracts given in my department are given to prominent members of the Conservative party. It suits our convenience to do so. They are the men best fitted to do the work and the fact that they are Conservatives has not prevented their getting it.
Further in the case of war, a good many of the purchases, especially of supplies like forage, were made by private bargain and arrangement.
Paragraph 4 in the 'Instructions for the Director of Navy Contracts,' says :
To insure the supply of articles of satisfactory quality, care must be taken to obtain them only from persons or firms of repute, not however excluding resort to persons and firms in a small way of business in suitable cases and for this purpose the system of limited tenders should be encouraged in preference to general invitation by advertisements.
That is the evidence of the assistant director of navy construction:
In such case, other matters being equal, the principle of excepting the lowest offer should prevail, i. e. that with regard to each particular class of articles you have a list of contractors from whom you invite tenders.
A. Yes. Almost invariably the lowest tender from any person on that limited list is accepted, because we put on one level all on the list.
Q. If you wanted an article at all urgently and the question of time was important, although^ the price was rather high, however, you might give it to a man who you were quite sure would be punctual.
A. Yes, it is occasionally done.
Tenders for construction work, fuel, provisions, food and forage, &c., and barrack services appear to be called for by public advertisement.
Just as is done in this country. Here is another important extract from the minutes of evidence of the Royal Commission on the South African war 1903-evidence of Mr. Alfred Major, Director of Army Contracts, page 267:
,, Q;	consider it necessary, in order
that the trade should be in a position to supply stores, that they should have a share Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
of the provision of those stores in times of peacer
A. Certainly; otherwise they are not prepared to meet our requirements. As regards quality and patterns, they vary in almost every instance from the ordinary trade pattern.
Just let me point out the full import of that answer. If you want to get supplies, you must make contracts with people who are in the habit of doing the work. In Canada where clothing, for instance, is not made by the government as it is in England, it is absolutely of the first importance that the government should deal with firms who are able to do the work and who will undertake to have the necessary plant and employees to do more work in the event of any emergency arising. This is a matter of the utmost importance and to which I do not think due consideration is given. So much for the system in England which is practically the same as that in Canada. Here is one other extract, in which perhaps my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) might be interested, as showing what is sometimes done in the mother country. I am quoting from page 6 of the minutes of evidence taken before the Commission on War Office Organization, 1901 :
Details of a case were given where the general officer commanding applied for the removal of the contractor's name from the list of those to whom tenders should be sent. The Secretary of State decided that the name should not be removed.
Whether that was political influence or otherwise I am not in a position to say. In that same evidence before the same commission, General Bulier said:
We are not particular enough with our contractors. We let men on the list who are probably very doubtful.
Here is a bit of evidence which is interesting. Everybody knows who Mr. Fleetwood Wilson is. He makes the following statement:
I made up my mind I would require say 100,000 yards of tartan. I would then put up to the director of contracts my demand. He would ask me who I would suggest as likely to supply that cloth at a reasonable price, of good quality and punctually delivered. I would then suggest certain firms which I knew
wkich I had reason to believe would serve
1 c^Par^^lenf' well give my reasons, and send them up to the director of contracts. The director of contracts in some instances suggests an allotment to other firms or the allotment of different quantities to the same firms. Eventuallv the director of contracts put all the machinery of putting out tenders and signing forms, etc., into work.
That will indicate the system which has been adopted in England after 100 or 200 years of experience. I have already stated that so far as our system is concerned, contracts for food supplies for the permanent force and annual camps and for fuel are

made only after tenders have been called for by public advertisement.
Now as to stores generally. Competitive tenders are usually obtained by circular letter just as is done in England from firms well and favourably known to the department as reliable and competent for the work they undertake. A list of such firms is kept in the contracts branch and the order or contract goes to the lowest tenderer unless good reason appears to ihe contrary, a very rare occurrence. Then the goods are manufactured and they are sent in; there is a branch of the contract branch known as the inspection branch. The goods are there subjected to the most careful inspection before acceptance, they undergo careful inspection by trained men, experts in regard to the various articles purchased. Articles found not equal to the standard are rejected. The inspector, after checking quantities and quality, reports the number accepted; and these are sent into ordnance stores'. The ordnance officer gives the director of contracts a receipt for them and enters them in his journal of receipts. A record of all receipts and issues from stores is kept; and every stage of every transaction of purchase from the delivery of the stores for inspection until they become unserviceable or are destroyed, is reviewed by an officer of the accounts branch whose business is the auditing of stores. All vouchers relative to the case are sent him.
Suggestions have been made that no care is taken of stores, that there is no tracing of the stores and that we never know what condition they are in or what quantity we have on hand. This is absolutely misleading and grossly unfair to the department. Two sets of ledgers are kept, one set locally at the points where the stores are, all over the country, and another set at Ottawa in the audit branch. Every six months those ledgers are exchanged and the most careful audit that could possibly be made is made constantly, and I believe it is perfectly effective.
Some years ago we had a discussion in this House with regard to contracts for stores. At that time there were present in this House two ex-Ministers of Militia, Sir Adolphe Caron and Mr. Tisdale. It so happened that when I came into office I had cancelled some contracts which had been entered into for a period of three years. In June, 1896, contracts had been made by Mr. Tisdale with certain contractors for considerable quantities of clothing for three years. One of those contracts was not to take effect until a year later, 1897. I submitted the question to the then Minister of Justice who said that such a contract was illegal because a contract could not be made for articles when the money to pay for them had not been voted by parliament. However that may be, the contracts were in due course cancelled. I inserted an advertisement in the public press in all the large
cities in Canada asking for tenders for about $70,000 or $75,000 worth of clothing which we required by the middle of April following. The advertisement was inserted.
I think, about October or November. What was the result? The result was that when the month of April arrived and the day arrived on which these goods should h/ave been delivered, none of them had been manufactured. I sent a man to the factory of the contractor and there discovered that he had not taken a single stitch and not bought the first yard of cloth. What was my position? Men like the Sanfords, whose firm had been awarded the contract which I had cancelled, had tendered for this contract on the new advertisement but had failed to secure it. Why? Because the man who obtained the contract, whose name I shall not mention, was on the verge of insolvency and in order to keep his head above water for a little longer thought that to have a government contract would materially help him and he put in a tender so low that he himself could not do the work. Then I was forced into this position that I had to go to the Sanford Company and ask them as a favour to make the goods which I required for the then approaching camps at their own price. I am bound to say that their price was as reasonable as could be expected and I think it was at the price at which he tendered for this contract. There is the result of my experience. I have under my hand the speeches and the warnings which Sir Adolphe Caron and Mr. Tisdale gave me across the floor of the House at the time these contracts were terminated by me, and I must admit that what they said proved to be absolutely true, and I have not, with the exception, I think, of one occasion since then, ever asked for public tenders by public advertisement for goods of that kind. What is the distinction? There is no difficulty about food products because we all know about them, and the competition is so keen that we are quite sure that the quality will be good and it is easy to ascertain whether it is or not. But in the case of military supplies such as clothing and arms of various kinds, there is a technical side, and somebody has got to learn how to make those articles. As a rule, they learn at the public expense. But I prefer to deal with reliable men whq have already learned, and about whose bona fides, and whose character and reputation as manufacturers, there is no doubt. We have on the list men of that kind. Then for some years past a very large part of our supplies of that kind have been purchased from the same people, and the Sanfords supply the principal amount.
Is it the intention of the bon. minister to continue giving contracts for military clothing in future without asking for tenders?

We ask for tenders, but in the way I speak of. I hope we shall not be required to advertise in the public newspapers. I do not want to go through again what I went through once before to my sorrow, and which was disastrous to the country, and put us to great inconvenience. I think it would have been much more disastrous if that particular party had been able to make the clothing, because I am sure it would not have been satisfactory, because he had never had any experience in work of that kind. Now, we have, as I say, a competent corps of inspectors. The most careful inspection is carried on as to the colour of the clothing, as to the character of the work, and as to the cut. We have in that inspection room sealed patterns with which everything that comes in is compared, and frequently a garment is literally cut to pieces in order to see that at least one or two of each lot that comes in are all right, from which the rest can be fairly judged. In the case of boots and shoes, a boot is cut in two, cut crosswise and cut lengthwise. I have seen the work done myself, and it is most thoroughly done by experts. In the case of blankets, they are tested to see if they are shoddy. We won't buy anything that contains shoddy. But if, after coming to the department, it shows any shoddy, it is returned, or paid for at a lower price. Then we have another check in addition to the director of contracts who is himself a specialist in a business way, and is watching prices constantly. In addition to the inspectors who are certainly specialists as to the value of goods and clothing, and who have the proper means of making an inspection, we have the price list of the War Office, the vocabulary, with which we can compare our prices with the prices at the War Office in England, adding the duty whatever it may be, and by that means we can come within a fraction of what the article is worth. We have in our department samples of clothing and samples of goods which are furnished to the War Office, and upon which these prices in the vocabulary are based.
I have already spoken of the audit of stores, and of the work done by the pay branch. I would like to say a word as to where these supplies come from. I am sure the committee will be glad to know that perhaps seven-eighths, at least three-forths of all the supplies purchased by the Militia Department are manufactured or supplied in Canada. In fact, with the exception of the artillery, of the guns, which are supplied at present in England, practically everything is supplied in Canada. I would like to read here just a word or two from a memorandum which was laid before the Mr. TALBOT.
Imperial Conference in 1907. It is a memorandum prepared by the then Quartermaster General, Sir Wm. Nicholson, who is now the chief of the General Staff, and practically the head next to the Minister of Army Council and by Mr. C. F. Madden, who was then Master General of the Ordnance:
It is most desirable that the area of supply of the warlike stores under reference

That is rifles, cannon, ordnance, everything.
-should be as wide as possible, and, therefore, the colonial government should be urged to arrange for local manufacture and provision, rather than to rely on the resources of the United Kingdom.
Well, we are doing that, and I hope the day will come, and come, soon, when cannon, and everything can be manufactured in this country. I may, however, say that at the present moment we are able to get all the limbers, ammunition waggons and carriages manufactured in Canada. They are being manufactured in this very city, and if any hon. member of the committee desires to spend an interesting half hour, I would advise him to go to the works of the Ottawa Car Company, and see the most creditable work that is being done there, and at a price as cheap, or nearly so, as the War Office pays; the price which we pay for those wagons is the War Office price with the duty added. I hope that in a few years we shall have not only a partially self-contained militia, as we have to-day to a very large extent, but that the militia, in so far at any rate as regards the supply of material of every kind, will be absolutely self-contained, and that everything can be manufactured in our own country. The importance of that I need not dwell upon, in the event of any trouble occurring. If any misfortune were to happen to the British fleet _our position would be very serious indeed if we were dependent entirely for our supplies on the other side of the Atlantic.
Before concluding my remarks I would like to call attention to a comparison which was made by General Sir Percy Lake, in a memorandum which I laid on the table of the House a year ago. a comparison showing the establishments of the organized units of the Canadian militia _ in 1895-6, in 1903-4, and 1908-9 respectively. I have also a comparative table to show the armament and equipment of the militia, the cadet corps and the rifle associations for the years 1895-6, 1903-4, and 1908-9. I will not detain the committee by reading these tables but I think it would be desirable, in order to make my statement complete, that they should be published in 'Hansard.'	,

Before the item is discussed I would like to refer to one rather important matter that the minister has not mentioned in his remarks this afternoon. I think the changes which he proposes for the militia show a great deal of forethought and study and will no doubt eventually work out, in a great many instances, for the betterment of the permanent corps, of the militia, and to the advantage of the country at large, and of the empire in general. But, as regards the formation of the imperial general staff, with ultimately a first and second line of defence and the formation of a corps for service abroad, I think he is to be congratulated on two points; in the first instance on the fact that the chief of the imperial general staff does not issue orders to the colonial general staff.
I do not say this because I think our colonial general staff are superior in any way, because I think possibly matters are reversed, but, from the fact that I think the leaders of the colonial general staff will, in this way, retain their own individuality and personality to a greater degree than if commanded by imperial officers. The other point of congratulation, I think, lies in the fact that the government has at last realized that Canada must be prepared to defend herself at home and not rely, as formerly, some members of the cabinet did, altogether on the Monroe doctrine. With the formation of an imperial general staff and with a first and second line of defence there will no doubt be some system of national defence with respect to our borders and seaports. I fully realize the fact that these are not matters for open discussion inside or outside the House, but there might be some method by which not all, but some members of the opposition, might be placed in touch with what is going on in that way. But I would urge on the minister a reform in the training of officers. Just see the contrast between the civil training and military training. Two young men from the same family go down to the city of Toronto. One goes through the university, where he is treated as a responsible individual and comes out with a degree which fits him for any walk in life. The other is a private in some company and he goes into a barracks, where he is treated as a child and comes out with a sergeant's certificate. Later on he has to go Back and qualify for a lieutenancy, and then go back again ,to qualify for a major, and then qualify again to take command. But his brother, who is a provisional officer, goes down and qualifies at once for a lieutenancy. But these young men, whether privates or officers, ought to don the cadet uniform and be put on an equal footing. They should go through the same training and let the best man in educational fitness come out ahead as in the old days, when all had to graduate as cadets.
Reference has been made by the minister and the hon. member for Sherbrooke to the sea coast defences of the nation. But to my mind, train the young men of the country in the use of the rifle and provide two quick firing guns for every com->any, and I care not how many millions *ross the border. I listened with great interest to the remarks of the minister, who went over the whole subject pretty thoroughly. In my opinion the most important feature of his policy is that of assisting the boys and girls in our schools by giving them more physical drill in the first place, and afterwards by teaching the boys how to handle the rifle. If the minister will carry out that policy, he will in a few years have achieved the great desideratum which *Lord Roberts is trying to obtain in England. He will have at his hand a trained body of young men ready to follow the standard if necessary and who have been trained in the use of the rifle and are able to shoot straight. And after all, in a country of such magnificent distances as Canada, and with such a sparse population, the most we can do is to have our young men so trained that if the call to arms is sounded they can take their places in the ranks and be something better than mere recruits. I think that is the very best thing the minister has offered us in his speech. Some very sensitive people make the objection that this would encourage militarism in the country and that our young people, who were drilled in the schools and taught to handle the rifle, would not feel content unless they went into active service, and if they could not find active service at home would find it elsewhere. I do notvthink there is anything in that objection. This matter of drilling in the schools is an old one on the other side of the Atlantic. When I was a boy, I was drilled twice a week for several years, and I do not think that inclined me to militarism to any great extent; and I am very glad there is a prospect of that system being taken up in all the provinces because it will furnish us a foundation for an army in the cheapest and most satisfactory way we can hope to get it.
As regards the question of rifles, I am inclined to believe it would be certainly a great advantage if all the imperial troops
had the same rifle. Next to that is the advantage of having a rifle in all the parts of the empire which will at all events take the same size cartridge, so that the ammunition which serves for one will do for the other.

Upon cursorily glancing through the report and the memorandum which have been distributed I find, in two or three places, a reference to the fact that the large increase in expenditure was necessitated by the garrisoning of Halifax and Esquimalt. I find that the total cost of the maintenance of the permanent corps at Halifax for the last fiscal year was $761,000 in round numbers, and at Esquimalt $103,000, making a total of $864,138. The total increase for the maintenance of the permanent corps for 1907-8 was $923,700-about $50,000 more than the total cost of the two stations of Halifax and Esquimalt combined. It is also stated in the memorandum accompanying the estimates that it was necessary to increase the officers and men of the permanent corps by about 1,500, and that to carry out the duties imposed by reason of the taking over of the two garrisons of Halifax and Esquimalt required a total of 3,311 men. I take it that it did not cost any more to keep the original 1,500 during the year 1907-8 than it previously did; that is to say that the taking over of the two garrisons of Esquimalt and Halifax would not make any difference as regards the first 1,500, so that if you cut

the total expenditure in two for the maintenance of Esquimalt and Halifax you will then find that you have about $432,000 of additional expenditure, while the increase for maintenance is $923,000, which makes a difference of something over $500,000. So far the debate seems to have been confined to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House who are in favour of the expansion of the military system in Canada. I feel I would be an unworthy representative of my constituency if I did not take advantage of this occasion to say that the people in the county I represent look with considerable disfavour upon any system which will tend to create and encourage in Canada what may be known a3 a military aristocracy. Now sir, this view possibly has been encouraged by the fact that for some reason or other the battalions from that part of the country had not been completed, with the result that when they arrived in Montreal they recruited them very largely from the wharf rats there. The military drill has been looked on as a sort of a joke. Possibly this is very largely due to the prevalence at the annual camps of the canteen. I submit to the Minister of Militia that the first thing necessary to encourage young men and especially farmers' sons to identify themselves with the militia, is to abolish the canteen at the drills because no mother [DOT]who has a respect for heT son, will permit that boy to go to the annual drills when she knows that the most he will learn will be to smoke cigarettes, drink whisky and mingle with the worst elements in the community. I offer this suggestion in no spirit of criticism of the estimates because it seems that the committee is unanimous in adopting the military policy as outlined by the minister. But I feel it is my duty, as a representative of the people of that 73
part of the country, to point out to the minister one of the great obstacles, to the encouragement of the right class of young men, the bone and sinew of the country, to attend the annual camps.

I agree with most of what my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) has said. I think that the fact thq,t captains are not as careful as they should be in the selection of men to take into camp has done the militia a great deal of harm, and that very often the fact that notorious characters are known to be included in these companies has prevented the enlistment of more worthy young men, such as my hon. friend refers to, farmers' sons. I think a good deal of amendment has taken place in that regard, but there is room for more. With regard to the canteen, we have been doing what we can to prevent that nuisance. The regulations are of the strongest kind. In some of the camps, at any rate, the officers are honestly endeavouring to carry out these regulations, _ but my hon. friend knows how difficult it is to control the sale of liquor. Liquor is brought in though it is against the law to sell it m the canteen. It seems impossible to exclude it. I hope that in all, and I certainly know that in many, of the camps, all measures possible are being taken to prevent the sale of intoxicating liquors.

ture from Barriefield to Kingston, you would be in danger of breaking through into the water. I think a new bridge could be constructed there at a comparatively small cost. The lake has a good, hard bottom, and the; water is comparatively shallow. I would also like to say to the minister that great advantage could be gained there by improving the channel of the Rideau canal. That would be an advantage to vessels, and it would also increase the harbour accommodation at Kingston. Hon. gentlemen who have visited Barriefield will remember that after you cross the bridge from Kingston there is quite a hill; that is government property. A couple of temporary tracks could be laid from that hill down to the bridge, the rock and stone material could be filled into the trucks, the loaded truck coming down to the bridge would carry the empty one back and with comparatively little expense a great portion of the bridge site could be filled in. I know that the city of Kingston owns a portion of the stock in the bridge, and I believe the government could come to terms with the city, construct a new bridge there and save money by the operation. While I do not like to suggest that convict labour should compete with free labour. I would call attention to the fact that near Kingston we have a penitentiary with a great many convicts in it, and I do not see why these convicts cannot be taken down to the neighborhood of the bridge and their services utilized for the purpose of filling in and reconstructing. I think that something along that line might be done and that convict labour might be employed to a partial extent in the work of reconstructing that bridge without very much fault being found by the general public. I trust that the minister will give this some consideration and I think that if it is considered from the standpoint merely of dollars and; cents the government can afford to reconstruct that bridge. One thing is absolutely certain and that is that a new bridge will have to be constructed there, very soon if you are going to have a crossing that will be of any avail for military purposes at all. Lumber is getting more and more expensive and I think the time is opportune to deal with those owning stock in the present bridge. You could look at the matter from the standpoint of the capitalization of the amount that you annually pay for the rent of the bridge, and, looking at it from a business point of view, I believe that that amount of money would more than construct a new bridge at Barriefield and give you something that would last for all time to come.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I desire to call the attention of the government and of the House to a matter of very general importance in order to elicit from the government some idea of what they intend doing in regard to this matter, the Co-operative Bill, which was adopted in this House last year and met with defeat in the Senate. Let me briefly explain the facts in connection with this very important measure. Some years ago I called the attention of the government to the advisability of giving effect in this country to some^ such legislation as has been adopted in most European countries and in other countries throughout the world in order to encourage co-operation, as a means of affording relief to the working classes, the . agricultural classes and poor people generally who are not in a position to combine into joint stock companies, the organization of which demands the expenditure at the very beginning of a very considerable amount of money. I pointed out at that time to the govern-Mr. FOSTER.
ment some of the remarkable successes that had been obtained in Europe by cooperative credit and loan societies, and at that time my hon. friend the Finance Minister promised that attention would be given to this subject. Subsequently in one of the following sessions I introduced a Bill providing for the organization of cooperation in this country among the working classes and the farming classes and generally upon the lines adopted for the legislation in England, combining with it, as far as possible advantageous provisions which are found in continental legislation. The Bill was explained when introduced, discussed on its second reading and the second reading was adopted by the House without dissent. The session was then advanced and acting under the advice of my hon. friend the Minister of Labour further progress in regard to the measure was deferred until the following session. At the beginning of the following session the Bill was again introduced. Its provisions were widely made known throughout the country and the introduction of that legislation received the general approval of the press and of all people who had given any attention whatever to the co-operative movement throughout the world. The Bill was again discussed as to its principles upon the second reading, it was favourably viewed by this House, the second reading was carried and it was referred for examination to a select Committee of this House composed of those members who had taken a particular interest in its introduction, including the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Justice, and the two members in the House who were more particularly supposed to represent the labouring classes.
I believe that most of the older members of this House have read the report of that committee. Its sittings extended over a considerable period and we had occasion to go fully into the question of co-operation, its necessity in this country, its utility and the details of the Bill. We heard witnesses of all kinds, men of eminent merit in regard to sociological subjects. We had the advantage of the testimony of His Excellency the Governor General. We also had agriculturists, financiers, the Deputy Minister of Labour who had given this matter very careful consideration and who furnished valuable information, Frofessor Shortt, and most of the principal employees of the Agricultural Department, in fact all the witnesses who could throw any light upon the subject. Their testimony was uniformly favourable to the passage of the measure we had under consideration. After the unanimous report of the committee upon that Bill, the government declared its intention of adopting the measure. I do not believe that any parliamentary committee throughout the

world has ever gone as fully into the question of co-operation as that Select Committee did. A committee in India has studied the question of ao-operation at perhaps greater length and made a fuller report, but this report was ample, it seems to me, to justify the position which the government took at that time, in making it a government measure. The Minister of Labour took charge of the Bill which afterwards came up in its regular turn for third reading. It was considered in Committee of the Whole and gone into at considerable length by that committee. It was then adopted unanimously by this House. It was then sent to the Senate and there the then Secretary of State, acting for the government, took up the Bill, and I must say that the Hon. Mr. Scott gave the subject matter of that legislation very considerable attention. He took communication evidently from cover to cover of the extensive report of the Select Committee of this House. The Bill was read the first time and explained by him in the Senate, read the second time and discussed and the principle of the Bill I believe was adopted without any dissentient voice. It was then sent to the Committee on Banking and Commerce of the Senate in order that certain representatives of the provinces and the secretaries of the Retail Merchants Association might be heard in regard to it.	__
The Bill remained in the committee of the Senate for four months. There were hearings of different parties; several of us who took great interest in the advancement of that legislation were heard and so were the representatives of the retail associations. I may say here that a very singular misapprehension as to the object of that legislation seems to have existed from the very beginning in the minds of those who were advancing the interests of the Retail Merchants Association. Very far from considering that measure as one to be enacted in the interests of the working classes, in the interest of the agricultural classes, and of poor people generally, they got it into their heads that the object of this legislation was to introduce into this country, in a disguised form, a vast aggregation of European capital in order to stifle the legitimate commerce of this country. How that idea happened to take possession of these people I do not know. I can only attribute it to the fact that there are in England two or more joint stock companies bearing the name of co-operative associations. I refer to the Civil Service Co-operative Stores and to the Army Stores, not co-operative in the sense in which we understand it, but joint stock companies properly so-called, declaring dividends, having a distribution of shares like all joint stock companies and never having been admitted, having, in fact, been refused admission to the co-operative union of England which gathers under its protection all the co-operative associations, properly so-called, of the British Isles. However, it may be that that opinion was entertained here, it found forcible expression by the representatives of the Retail Merchants Association before the committee of the Senate. We, who are anxious to establish the facts, sought vainly to persuade the members of the committee that this was an entire misapprehension and misunderstanding. There were also heard before the committee of the Senate, representatives from the province of Quebec and of the province of Ontario. Mr. Mulvey, assistant Provincial Secretary of Ontario, urged strongly at that time that there was legislation in Ontario providing fully for the organization of just such co-operative societies as we had in view, and which was then under consideration. The views expressed there by Mr. Mulvey seemed to have prevailed with the committee of the Senate, although he was undoubtedly mistaken, and since these events have transpired a co-operative society here in Ottawa that has sought to be organized under the laws of the province of Ontario has found that there is no legislation in Ontario providing for such an organization, and they have been promised, I believe, by the government of that province, that some relief would be afforded them by legislation to be introduced during the present session. The Bill, Mr. Speaker, came back to the Senate after this long delay and towards the close of the session. The committee reported that they recommended that the preamble of the Bill be not adopted. It was pointed out in the discussion which took place in the Senate and to which I will refer briefly

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) will allow me I would point out that it is irregular to refer to a debate in the Senate. Bourinot says:
It is a part of the unwritten law of parliament that no allusion should he made in one House to the debates of the other chamber, a rule always enforced by the Speaker with the utmost strictness.
He adds, however :
It is perfectly regular, however, to refer to the official printed records of the other branch of the legislature, even though the document may not have been formally asked for and communicated to the House.
What I was going to say applies to past debates as 1 have often heard past debates of the Senate quoted in this Chamber.
The rule seems to make no distinction and I thought I would call the hon. gentleman's attention to it.

At any rate, by your ruling, I will be permitted to refer to the official decisions of the Senate.
duty to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to what seems to be the proper practice.

I venture to suggest that the rule does not apply to debates of past sessions in the Senate any more than it applies to such debates in the House of Commons. As a mater of fact, it has been the constant practice in this House to refer to debates in the Senate and any enforcement of the rule would prevent a single reference to the many valuable opinions expressed by the members of the Senate from confederation down to the present time. That would seem to be an extreme view. For example, in the debate upon the Autonomy Bill in 1905, there were constant references to the debates which had taken place in the Senate in 1872 or 1873, and all these references took place without the slightest objection and without the slightest idea that any hon. gentleman so referring to them was out of order. I would venture to think that the rule has not the wide application which is sought to be given to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the rule respecting past debates in the House of Commons and the rule respecting debates in the Senate have different objects. The rule respecting past debates in the House is designed to prevent the repetition of a matter which the House has already dealt with The rule respecting debates in the Senate is on the_ higher ground of protecting the proper privileges of the Senate, but an evasive manner is sometimes adopted in order to discuss past debates of the Senate.

I would not be inclined so to regard it. The real object of the rule is to prevent members of the House of Commons answering arguments which have been addressed to the Senate in the same session, when matters of a similar nature might be under consideration in both Houses at the same time. It might be extremely inconvenient and probably undignified that any such course as that should be adopted. Any reference to a debate in the Senate must be respectful, must not lack in that proper respect which is due to a co-ordinate branch of the legislature. Subject to that I never knew that there could be any possible objection to referring to a debate which had taken place in the Senate in a former session.

Bourinot also says :
