I have no intention of being more severe than is necessary, but I thought it was my Mr. SPEAKER.

I will not attempt to evade your ruling, Mr. Speaker; in fa/ct, I may say that it saves me the trouble of calling to the attention of this House some opinions expressed in the other Chamber that would cause a good deal of surprise to members of this House who have given some attention to. constitutional questions. It appears from the very nature of the proceedings held in the Senate that a certain number of these hon. gentlemen took the trouble to study the report of the Select Committee in this House upon that important subject, whereas some others thought they could effectually dispose of this important measure without giving themselves the trouble to study the matter at all. The then Secretary of State gave the matter much attention in the Senate and supported the measure in pursuance of the policy adopted by the government, and Senator Beique, of Montreal, suggested some important amendments intended to remove all doubt as to the constitutionality of our legislating in the matter. There was placed before the Senate at that time an opinion which had been, shall I say attempted to be obtained, from the Minister of Justice, as to the constitutionality of this measure, and in that opinion, which forms part of the records of parliament, the Minister of Justice said:
I recognize that it is my duty as official legal adviser of the Governor General and legal member of His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada to advise the Crown upon all matters of law referred to me by the Crown, and to advise the beads of the several departments of the government upon all matters of law connected with such departments, but it would seem to me presumption on my part to offer advice to either House of parliament or to .a standing committee of the Senate, especially when among its members there are many honourable and learned gentlemen more competent than I to form an opinion upon any doubtful matter of law.
Moreover the Bill referred to has been passed by the House of Commons and in that view it would ill become a member of that House to question the constitutional power of parliament to enact legislation of this character.
There is no doubt that a very strong lobby was Tesorted to in the upper House for the defeat of that measure, and I have heard since with much approval strong condemnation of that system of lobbying particularly as applied to the other Chamber. At any rate, the final result of the discussion upon the motion made in the Senate that this singular conclusion at which the Committee on Banking had arrived should not be adopted by the Senate, but that the Bill should be referred to the

Committee of the Whole for further examination was defeated by a vote of 19 to 18. The preamble of the Bill, as the Secretary of State had seen fit to alter it, simply declared that it was desirable in order to promote the interests of the working and agricultural classes of Canada to provide them with a legal method of organizing into co-operative societies. I may state for the information of the House, and it is well known to the government, that since the subject of co-operation has become a live issue in this country many people interested in the public welfare have endeavoured to promote legislation of this kind. The Labour Congress of Canada at its annual convention has been for some years passing resolutions in favour of this legislation. Similar resolutions have been adopted at meetings of clergymen of all denominations, and many other economic associations have taken a warm interest in the matter. It is not surprising then that the action of the Senate caused very great dissatisfaction among the members of the labour congress, and at the last annual meeting held in Halifax in September last the following resolution was unanimously adopted :
Moved by delegate Adam Anderson of the Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners of Montreal:
That this congress views with profound astonishment the colossal ignorance of the Dominion Senate of the modern conditions of economic progress, in opposing co-operation which has been established in Britain, France and Germany for fifty years with such distinguished success in cultivating the highest qualities and developing the highest ideas of citizenship.
Be it resolved that this congress demands that the Dominion government should incorporate in our laws the inalienable right of our people so to combine.
Concurred in unanimously.
I have only to add this: At the beginning of this session a pamphlet was circulated among the members of this House, which purports to emanate from the secretary of the Retail Merchants' Association, whose office is in the city of Toronto, and that pamphlet is entitled:	'The system
adopted by co-operative societies exposed. How the people are deceived by so-called co-onerative societies.' I shall not take up the time of the House by quoting at length from that pamphlet, but I must say that it displays a very extraordinary degree of ignorance in regard to the success of the co-operative movement on the continent of Europe. Everybody knows that that movement has been attended with marvellous success; that at the present moment the greatest efforts are being made in England to extend it; and that in Ireland the efforts of Sir Horace Plunkett in the direction of agricultural co-operation have changed the entire economic aspect
of that country. I cannot qualify this pamphlet otherwise than as a scurrilous document. It casts very grave reflections on the attitude taken by this House with regard to that measure. It states that the measure had been surreptitiously forced through the House and that it did not receive from the House of Commons that treatment which I must say in my long experience as a member this House always accords to measures of this importance. Then, this pamphlet caps the climax by alleging that the object of the legislation was to advance my own interests and the interests of those who manifested some concern in the progress of this legislation. The pamphlet further states that my object as a member of this House in promoting the legislation was in order that I might become an officer of a joint-stock co-operative society organized in my own province. I have never thought it worth while until now to deny that statement. I deny it now. In the expectation that this measure would not meet with defeat in the Senate, numbers of working men in my own constituency in the city of Montreal were prepared to organize societies. In my own constituency one was actually organized and has since been legalized under the incomplete provincial legislation which we have upon this subject, and I consented to become the honorary president of that society. That is the extent of the financial interest _ which 1 have had in this great movement in connection with which not one of those who took any interest in it had any financial consideration in view, I am sure. The pamphlet goes on to allege that His Excellency the Governor General, who himself appeared as a witness before the committee of investigation in our House, had some financial motive, inasmuch as lie had been president of the Co-operative Union of England, a union which, as everybody knows, has no financial operations in view at all, but merely the promotion of ideas favourable to the spread of co-operation.	_	_	_
There is much more I might insist^ upon, but I do not wish to take up the time of the House. .The question is, what is the government going to do? I think the government, since the idea of this legislation was mooted, has taken a fair and prudent position in regard to it. Is it going to be said that a law desired by everybody who knows anything of co-operation throughout the Dominion of Canada, asked for by resolutions and deputations of all kinds, asked for by the congress of labour, approved of generally by the people throughout the Dominion-is it going to be said that a law of that kind is going to be defeated by the action of nineteen members of the Senate, who it is evident have not bestowed upon the question the attention which it deserves? I hope not. I think the govern-

ment should courageously persist in its course, re-introduce the measure, make it as perfect as possible, and place this country upon the same footing as other countries in regard to this important movement. It has been alleged that the provinces have jurisdiction in this matter. In regard to the formation of societies for certain objects purely local, the provinces might be considered to have jurisdiction; but the point insisted upon at all times when this legislation has been considered, has been that without the benefit of banking operations, we cannot have co-operation in its true and legitimate field of beneficent work. That feature can only be conferred on co-operation through the instrumentality of this legislation. It has been argued, I think very properly, that this being legislation essentially for the benefit of workingmen and the agricultural, classes throughout the Dominion, we have jurisdiction to legislate in favour of these classes and to give them the benefit of a cheap and easy mode of organization in co-operative societies. I believe that view was shared at the time by the Minister of Justice, who was present in our committee, and suggested some improvements in the Bill as it was first received in the committee. That view was strongly pressed on the senators; and if hon. members will take the trouble to read the debate that took place in the Senate when the Bill was finally disposed of, they will find that no valid or real argument was put forth against that view. Under these circumstances, I hope the government will take the measure up once more, and I have confidence that the Upper House will not again in this important matter seek to defeat the will of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say just a word or two on this very important question. The hon. gentleman has always been a very ardent apostle of the principle of co-operation in this House, and I must probably attribute to him the fact that the Bill which I introduced last year was so unanimously adopted by the House of Commons. The government has not wavered in its view of the usefulness of the co-operative movement. Last year the government decided to take up this measure and pass it. It was not at first a government measure, but it became a government measure after the report of the special committee appointed to deal with the question. When the Bill went to the other Chamber, it met with very persistent opposition at the hands of some senators belonging to both sides of politics. Views, and very strong views, were expressed against the jurisdiction of this par-lament to deal with this question, and the senators who held those views were reinforced by the very active opposition which came from the retail merchants of the Dominion.

Let me say at once that favourable as I am to the principle of this Bill-and I recognize the very many advantages that can be derived from such a measure by the labouring classes-yet I have been impressed since last year with the very strong feeling -it may be a prejudiced feeling-which exists in some parts of our community against the passing of this measure by the federal parliament. I have not wavered from the position I took last year, and I shall be quite ready to support a Bill of the same nature in the House; but there is such a thing as provincial rights, and in my opinion, which I believe is the opinion of the majority of the members of this House, we must respect not only what we term provincial rights, but even provincial prejudices. It is my opinion that this parliament has complete iurisdiction in this matter; but we find that the largest and wealthiest province of the Dominion, the province of Ontario, with another large province, the province of Quebec, represented by their executive, strenuously opposed the passing of this measure when it reached its final stage in the Senate last year. Now, the two Attorney Generals of Ontario and Quebec may be wrong, and I do not discuss the opinion which they expressed last year through their respective representatives before the Senate; but I say it is the duty of this government to respect not only what they assert to be their rights, but even what we may think are only their prejudices. At all events that is my view on the broad question of provincial rights. It may be that within a few months, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, represented by their respective governments, after careful study of this measure, may come to the conclusion that it is one which ought to become law. I may say to my hon. friend that my sympathies are' with this movement, but we must admit that the sentiment in favour of cQ-operation is not yet very pronounced throughout the Dominion. I however am pleased to see that it is perhaps more developed in the province of Quebec than in any other. Although to a certain degree the principle of co-operation has been adopted in certain centres of the province of Ontario, it has not yet become accepted as a general principle in the country at large.
As Minister of Labour, I have received no petitions from the great provinces of the west or from the maritime provinces, but I have received a limited number from the province of Quebec and a few from the province of Ontario. I myself am in favour of the principle, but as the two large provinces are actually opposed to the passage of this measure, I think we can let the matter stand until some progress in education on the subject has been made. The discussions which took place before the select committee and those which took

place in this House last year and in the Senate will no doubt contribute towards the passing of this measure finally in a few months hence. I rose simply to say that my sympathies are still with the principle of co-operation, but that a little delay will not hurt this measure after all, and any legislation we may pass will not be only for a year or two, but will be for ever if once the principle of co-operation is admitted by both Houses.

The history of this question of co-operation embodied in the legislation of last session has been thoroughly given by my hon. friend who introduced the measure. As a member of the select committee on that subject, and having had some considerable experience with the movement in the old country, I may say that I was very much disappointed at the attitude taken by the Senate last year. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) has suggested that the question of provincial rights may have entered into the consideration of this matter. I am not aware that any consideration of the rights of the provinces to enact legislation of this kind was seriously debated in t]A Senate at all. It is true that the representatives from Ontario and Quebec who met the select committee of the Senate questioned the right of the Dominion government to enact _ such legislation. No doubt the distributive principle of co-operation is a matter of provincial right and one which the provinces have exercised. In Nova Scotia they have an Act providing for co-operative societies in the distribution of goods to their members. In British Columbia they have the same law and also in Ontario. But the question of banking the profits of co-operative distribution was never supposed to be provided for by provincial legislation, and the object of this Bill is to provide^ for_ banking privileges by Dominion legislation. The object of the legislation is to make it possible for any association, in the distribution of goods to its members, to have the banking profits in the sale of these goods, and every authority consulted on this legislation has declared it was necessary to come to this House to get that kind of legislation. I just want to say that it is a surprise to me, after eighty years experience in Britain-for it is eighty years since similar legislation was passed in England by the voluntary associations co-operative movement-to find in this country objection to a principle enacted and put in operation eighty years ago in the old country. A lobby and agitation against the movement was organized by the retail dealers, particularly of Ontario, or it may be perhaps the Dominion organization. There was a similar agitation of England retail dealers some twenty-five years ago against the enactment of similar
legislation. But the principle is plain and easy. If half a dozen men are entitled to have special legislation to co-operate their wealth for the purpose of carrying on a certain business and supplying the needs of the public in the operation of that business, has not the public the right to provide its own needs? Why should it not have legislation to supply its own needs as effectively as a limited liability company or other organization? It would be interesting, if I thought it reasonable to occupy the time of the House in so doing, _ to discuss the industrial and sociological benefits of the principle of co-operation in Great Britain. Every man has the right to study that for himself, hut the right to have social organizations to carry on commerce of this kind and invest their own profits is a legitimate one. I do not know what the government will do. It would be unseemly to take the Senate by the throat and make them do what we think_ they ought to do, but in that connection I noticed a little hesitation on the part of the Postmaster General regarding the authority of this parliament, which I do not think he showed as a member of the select committee years ago. It looked as if he were on the down grade on this question.
Last year, as a member of the select committee, my hon. friend was present and supported the Bill enthusiastically, and, if I am not mistaken, combatted the contention that this parliament had no right to enact legislation of this kind. The question as to the right of this) parliament to deal with legislation covered by the banking clauses of this Bill was never a serious question before that select committee, and, certainly, no doubt was expressed in that committee as to that right. I hope the Dominion government will realize the importance of this measure and take the responsibility of using every legitimate influence to secure its enactment. Even suppose for one moment that it is entirely, exclusively, within the jurisdiction of the provinces to legislate on the subject of co-operative societies established to distribute goods among their members, the fact remains that there can be no successful co-operative movement which has various forms in various provinces; the co-operative movement, in order to be successful, must be a national movement, it must be free to extend its operation to every part of the country. The history of the co-operative movement in England has demonstrated that fact. There, they have federal legislation and rights that cover the whole country. A.nd, in my experience, it is utterly impossible for the co-operative movement to exist and be successful unless it has the necessary federal legislation whereby it can operate throughout the whole Dominion. I merely wish to say these few words in support of this Bill, and if this government can do

anything to promote and influence the Senate to pass it, I think they should use their influence to that end.

I wish to bring to the notice of members of this House an article which appeared in the Toronto 'Evening Telegram' of March 8 in regard to immigration to this country:
Immigrfuit Tide Again - Three Hundred
strike City-Pitiful disappointment at the
Union Station [DOT]- Some go on to Western
Ontario, but many remain here.
About 300 immigrants from the old land arrived at the Union Station this morning. Two hundred and eleven arrived by special C.P.R., and 100 came through by the Grand Trunk. Many who arrived by the C.P.R. remained in Toronto, while the balance, with those of the G.T.R., will be distributed in the western towns of Ontario.
Have Little Money.
There was scarcely $100 in the party that remained in Toronto. One man had $50 of this. The British Welcome League took charge of about 15 families, and will provide for them until they are placed.
A few friends who have been in Canada for about a year met the party, and when they informed the strangers that there was no work here they appeared very much disappointed.
One man with a wife and six children, when told this, wept, because he had no money. He came out here, he said, because they told him in the old country that he would not be in Canada 24 hours before he would have lots of work. This man did not have a dollar.
A number of the men round the Union Station provided the children with breakfast.
I suppose there must be some government department that is responsible for this condition of things, and I think the House is entitled to an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unfortunately, I was not able to hear what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Russell) said at the beginning of his remarks. I take it that there is complaint that a number of immigrants arrived who were not possessed of the amount of money required by the regulations. I can only say that the statement will be given full consideration and an inquiry will be made. I beg to assure my hon. friend and the House that it is our intention to see to it that the regulations are complied with.

I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister to a despatch concerning an alleged conditional ratification of the International Waterways Treaty by the United States Mr. RALPH SMITH.
Senate. I do not know whether this despatch has been brought to the right hon. gentleman's attention or not.
Washington, D.C., Mar. 4.-Senator William Alden Smith of Michigan won another brilliant victory to-day when the Senate ratified the Canadian Boundary and Waterways Treaty with a resolution attached to meet his objections. This action is considered in Washington as insuring to Sault Ste. Marie, Mich., her rightful share of the available waterpower in St. Mary's river.	_	_
The fight over the waterway question in regard to the Soo proposition has been the subject of bitter controversy at times, and the Michigan senator was pitted against some of the strongest debaters of the upper House, but he won his point after fighting stubbornly and bringing into play a diplomacy that even his best friends did not believe him capable. The victory has placed him without doubt in the ranks of the legislative leaders at the Capitol. He is a force to be reckoned with.
The first part of the despatch is the part to which I wish to call attention. I would ask the Right Hon. the Prime Minister if he is aware that, in the ratification of that treaty there was attached any resolution or limitatWl such as is stated in the despatch Naturally, we who are so much interested in the development of the water-power, and wish to conserve all that belongs to Canada, are very anxious to know exactly what has been done.

I may inform my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) that the information contained in the despatch is, I will not say in all particulars but in its essential points, accurate. The treaty has been ratified, but with a rider which materially interferes, as I understand it, with the disposition of the water in the St. Mary's river. The question rests there at the present time. I may say that the treaty, though passed by the Sena'e has not been ratified by the Sovereign of this country. We are this very day sending a despatch to England to have the treaty laid on the table of the House, so that parliament may know exactly what are its terms. I hope to have this before many days are over.
Has the Minister of Agriculture the remaining schedules with regard to the flat increase of $150 to the civil servants?

I believe that the schedule for the House of Commons is about ready to be laid on the table. The Senate schedule I have not yet received. Until I get both of these, I cannot go on. The schedules for

all the departments are prepared-have
been for some time.
It appears that the legislative body itself is the one that is retard ing legislation. What is the trouble?

I do not know that I can lay the blame on anybody-if there is any blame. The Speaker and the clerk have been working on the schedule, and it was referred to the Committee on Internal Economy. That body has dealt with it, and I understand that it is now ready to be laid on the table.

I may state to my hon. friend that to-morrow, before we go into Supply, I propose to make a short statement with reference to what I consider certain irregularities and injustices in the administration of the new Civil Service Act. I shall not propose a motion, but simply make a statement.

I desire to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a matter relating to this House which should be remedied. This morning I came here to go to the restaurant for my breakfast at the usual hour, 8.30, and found the elevator to the restaurant out of business. After waiting some ten or fifteen minutes I went round to the other elevator at the main entrance but it was not running. I saw the chief messenger, Mr. Dube, and he told me they did not start the elevator until nine o'clock, that the Public Works Department did not send the man here until that hour. I waited until about nine o'clock when the one at the dining room was put in operation. It seems a pity that these elevators should not be started before nine o'clock in the morning. The men in the Public Works Department should start work at seven o'clock as other labouring men do and the elevators should commence to operate at that hour. It was out of order this morning when the committee met and we had to use the Senate elevator. No one wishes to climb three flights of stairs to go to his breakfast. The Minister of Public Works should look into the matter and see that the service is improved.

The elevator at the main entrance has been out of order a couple of times this session, and last year it fell several times so that a number of members narrowly escaped injury. An elevator that gets out of order every few days should be specially inspected in order to avoid accidents.

I am not complaining about the elevator not running before eight o'clock, as it would be of 74
little use to me, but I wish to emphasize what the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) has said. The elevator at the main entrance is hardly a safe one, it is out of commission almost every day. The engineer in charge is constantly attempting repairs to it but he does not seem to be successful. The Minister of Public Works should at once call in competent men and see that the elevator is made safe; it is not safe now.

I shall see that attention is given to the matter.
Motion agreed to and House went into Committee of Supply.
Annapolis harbour improvements, ice piers, $15,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: Of this amount $25,000 is a revote. The object of this improvement is to arrest the flow of ice into the harbour and so permit shipments from Annapolis in the winter season. There are to be a number of piers with substructures of closefaced, stone-filled cribwork, and concrete superstructures in the Annapolis river.
Is this the winter port business?
The same matter that we discussed last year.
The port being some miles above Annapolis.
No, Annapolis is quite a shipping port.
What has been one so far? Last year we did not get any very definite information as to the utility of, and consequently the necessity for, this outlay.

I think my hon. friend is in error. At the last session of parliament I quoted from reports in the House showing what it was hoped to accomplish by this work, and I was of the opinion that I convinced the majority of the committee that the work was necessary. Since that time tenders were called for the work but nothing has been done and we have determined upon calling for new tenders. An advertisement is now in the newspapers calling for new tenders for the work, so that all we have actually done is to purchase the creosoted timber.
What was the trouble with the old tenders?
The contractors refused to sign the contract.
What were the figures?

The tender was $34,400. The lowest tenderers were Reid and Archibald, of Halifax, but when we called upon



them to sign the contract they declined to do so unless we would insert a clause binding the government to assume certain risks as to the work. We declined to alter the terms of our proposed contract, they declined to sign it, and it was necessary to call for new tenders.
It is unusual for a contractor to refuse to sign a contract unless the government would assume the risks. What reasons did they advance?

That would be the risk of the work being destroyed during construction. An ordinary contract requires that the work must be completed by the contractor and we declined to accede to the wishes of the contractor.

That again raises the question as to what are the particular difficulties there. If there is such a menace that the contractor wishes to ensure himself, is not that a very great menace to the works after they are completed? There must be some abnormal conditions which are different from those at most places. I should think it would tend to make the whole thing risky even after the contractor had got it off his hands.

The engineers do not think so. They think that the work when once completed will stand all right. There was a second tender, that of H. M. Putnam and F. W. Clark, who did not insist upon any such condition in the contract, and who would have been willing to have taken the contract without it.
What were their figures?
Their tender was on the basis of a force account with ten per cent added.
The minister objected to that form of tender?
Yes.
Has the minister any of the correspondence showing what the would-be contractors thought to be the extraordinary elements entering into this work and which they thought constituted the risk?

I have not, but my recollection is that they expressed the opinion _ that there might be difficulty in completing the work; that is to say, that during the progress of the work and before it had been completed, it might be destroyed by the action of the tides, and they wished a condition put in that the risk should be assumed by the government. With regard to the other question, the opinion of the engineers is that when the work is once completed it is as likely to stand as any ordinary harbour work.

Will the minister give us the particulars of the tender, showing Mr. PUGSLEY.
just what the tenderer proposed to do? I have not in my mind a very clear idea of what this structure is and the terms of the tender would make that clear.
I will draw my hon. friend's attention to the contract, which provides for three piers just a little above the harbour of Annapolis.
In the river?
Yes, in the river. I suppose it can be called the harbour; it is just above Annapolis.
Do these three piers extend across the river the whole distance?

The whole scheme is to build either eight or ten piers-I am not quite sure-which are to extend all the way across the river. These three piers are to be built first at an estimated cost of $34,400. In addition to that there is the cost of creosoted timber, amounting to $12,619.24. That would make a total estimated cost of $47,019.24. besides which there are some other charges of superintendence. &e., amounting to about $3,400.
That would be about $50,000 for the three piers?
The total estimated cost is $50,000 for the three piers.
Then it is proposed that there shall be ten piers? That means that your total cost will he $160,000 or $170,000.
The estimated total cost of ten piers is $123,500.
Three of them cost about $50,000. but whether some of them are larger than others I do not know.
T think some of the others are somewhat smaller.
It mav be that they are, but the minister has not determined that in his own mind.
I have the engineer's estimate of $123,500 for the ten piers.

To which we pay a certain amount of deference, but we always find in the end that it is exceeded. Does the minister feel justified in taking $160,000 of the people's money to construct ice piers above the harbour in the Annapolis river? What are the advantages set forth to the minister that has brought him to embark upon that expenditure of public money at this particular time?

I may say to the hon. gentleman that the understanding with regard to the building of this pier was arrived at before I became minister. That understanding was arrived at after very careful consideration, after very careful surveys and after it had been determined that

the work would be a. useful one. What I had to do when I became minister was to endeavour to carry out the understanding which had been arrived at. I made inquiry with regard to the work and I was convinced that there would be a justification for it. Annapolis is an important shipping point. The shipments from there of lumber, apples, and other products, I believe, are quite large. It is believed that by the construction of these ice piers the river at Annapolis-what, perhaps, might not improperly be called the harbour of Annapolis- would be greatly improved, that these joiers will form a barrier against the drift ice that comes down wdth the tide in the winter season and that the harbour will be kept open during the winter. I believe that from Annapolis down to the mouth the river is open in the winter time; so that it is expected that vessels will be able to come there with safety in the winter season.

The minister says that he feels convinced, but he has not 'said anything to the committee to convince it that we should vote the amount of money which we are asked to vote and which will involve an expenditure of $160,000 or $170,000. He speaks of winter navigation. What are the possibilities of winter shipment out of Annapolis? One other point and it is this: The minister said that he found that his predecessor had practically come to an agreement; therefore, he did not consider that lie ought to revise it. An agreement with whom? It seems to me that the public interest is paramount and that a minister, coming in and finding that an arrangement is under way, is not bound to carry out that arrangement, unless it is interprovincial or international, or something of that kind. The main point is to find out what it is proposed to do. If there is the possibilities of making Annapolis a winter port we might expend $160,000 or $170,000 upon it. But at this particular juncture in our history does not the minister think that this is one of the things that might wait for a year, wait for two years, wait for a century for that matter?

I have not the lccal knowledge with regard to this work that would probably satisfy the curiosity of my hon. friend, but I recall very clearly a delegation from the county of Annapolis visiting Ottawrn some few years ago, and among the members of that delegation Who were especially anxious that this work should be undertaken by the government and who canvassed the support of all of us from Nova Scotia was Mr. Geo. E. Corbett, Conservative candidate in Annapolis in the last election. I am quite sure that that gentleman was very earnest in his advocacy, and that he felt convinced that he was asking the government, through the Department of Public Works, to inaugurate some-74i
thing that would be of great public benefit to the county and to the province of Nova Scotia.

We were told with reference to that famous Aylesworth ditch that Liberals as well as Conservatives had asked for it and it was supposed that settled the whole question. Does it make one pin's difference whether the demand for a public work is made by Liberals or Conservatives? Is not the real question: Is this an expenditure absolutely necessary in the public interest and if not absolutely necessary is it such an advisable expenditure that in these hard times we should take $170,000 of the money of the people for it?
Only one-third of that at present.

The minister is enough of a business man to know that if he commences to build a house he has to keep in mind the total expenditure and not the cost of the cellar wall which he may begin with. There are hundreds of instances in which expenditures have been cut off this year because the debt is increasing, the interest charge jumping by the millions, and the treasury depleted. I venture to say that no solid interest will be affected to the extent of anything worth considering if this work is left over until we get so much money that we want to waste it as we have been doing for some years past. At this period it is an outrage to be called upon to spend that amount of money on the harbour of Annapolis in the way of ice piers, and probably provincial bridges afterwards.

I may say that about thirty miles from Annapolis the Drummond Company have a large iron proposition and they wish to bring their iron to Annapolis for shipment. They have represented to me and to the government that they would build the piers and pockets to accommodate this trade provided the harbour was improved. Otherwise they feared their piers would be destroyed. We are spending money on the harbours of St. John and Halifax and other harbours in the Dominion to make them available for the shipment of the produce of the country, and this harbour at Annapolis is just as valuable as any of them to the extent of the interests it will serve. The improvement will accord a safe winter harbour for shipping and it will protect the wharfs already built as well as other wharfs which will be necessitated by the growing trade of that part of the country. The matter was gone into very fully last year by the minister and by other members of the House and no very great .objection was manifested towards this appropriation. I may say that about 140 coastwise vessels and 50 or 60 foreign going vessels load at Annapolis. It is essential to the interests of the district that this work should be done.
How many vessels load there in the winter ?
There is one loading there now and another loaded in January, but under present conditions it is not safe for them as the harbour is peculiarly situated and they are in danger from the ice.

Last year I asked if there were any statistics as to material damage being done to shipping from these ice floes and I did not get any information on the point. If there is any record of actual damage in that respect I would like to get it now, because if no great damage has been done in the past this is a pretty expensive way of going about remedying it. Are the vessels which ply to Annapolis ocean-going vessels ?

A few years ago there was a great deal of ice from one end of the river to the other and it froze over. Below the frozen part there was open water and a large steamer came in from Great Britain and discharged her load of coal on the ice and took a load of lumber and apples. That was in February and that was the only time the harbour was frozen over.
Is the apple crop of the Annapolis valley shipped to Europe via Annapolis ?
Some of it.
What proportion ?
I cannot say. If the harbour were available a larger part of the crop would find its way to Europe via Annapolis.
I was under the impression that the apple crop was exported from other ports.
That is so, but some of it is shipped from Annapolis and more would be shipped were the harbour improved.
When were tenders called for this work ?
I think in the early part of last summer.
Has the contract been let ?

No. As I stated, tenders were called and Reid and Archibald being the lowest the contract was sent to them for signature but they declined to, sign unless we should make certain modifications which we refused to do. In consequence of their refusal we are asking for new tenders.
Did Reid and Archibald send a certified cheque?
They did.
Did you return their cheque?
No.
You have it yet?
Yes.
You intend to hold it?
Yes, for the present.
They have done a great deal of public work?
Yes.
They are people you know very well?
Yes, very reliable contractors.
What is the reason you did not have them enter into the contract?

The reason was, as stated before, that they had some doubts apparently as to whether they would be able to complete the work. In all hydraulic work there is more or less danger, and they wore not willing to take the risk of completion. They wanted the Crown to take the risk of the plans and of the work standing until it was completed. I refused to assume that risk; I wanted to hold the contractors to the performance of the contract and the completion of the work, and in consequence of our not being able to agree on a modification of the contract as they desired, we have now called for new tenders.
What was the amount of their tender?

If I am rightly informed, the principal reason for this appropriation has not yet been dwelt upon to any extent. As I understand, the principal reason for erecting these piers across the estuary of the Annapolis river is to enable a provincial bridge to be built upon them at some future date. If that is the case, it seems to me that the vote is being obtained more or less under false pretenses. I would like to know from the minister whether there have been any negotiations with the provincial government or any member of the provincial government or with any member of this House in regard to the use of these piers for the purposes of a bridge?
There have been no negotiations with me, and none with the government that I am aware of.

There have been cases in which parliament has been hoodwinked into the construction of piers which were to be used for the purposes of a bridge. In the county of Terrebonne back of the Island of Montreal, this government was induced to build, in a river, eight or ten concrete piers which could not possibly be
i

reached by any boat within four or five miles, and where all access was cut off by a railway half a mile below. There has never been a boat to these piers, nor is there any expectation that a boat will ever go there. That was a case where this government, under the guise of building piers! as an aid to navigation, obtained a vote of money from parliament to aid the local authorities in building a bridge.

Perhaps it might not be but of place if I quoted from a report of the resident engineer at Halifax, Mr. Dod-well, who is an experienced engineer and has been in the department for a good many years, and who deals with the subject from the standpoint of harbour improvements.
Under the date of March 15, 1903, the resident engineer at Halifax reports that he had the opportunity of making a satisfactory inspection of runs of ice during the winter of 1903, and that he saw a representative one on the 25th of February of that year. The river as far as could be seen was full of ice from shore to shore, in cakes and sheets of all sizes, and in thickness from a few inches to six or seven feet. While he stood on the uppermost wharf on the Annapolis side, a large field came down in the last hour of the up-tide, caught on the wharf on which he stood, and lodging against the Granville foreshore, remained fixed and stationary until the flood-tide broke and took it up the river again. This he takes to be good evidence that a line of piers such as outlined in his plan and report of Jan. 18, 1902, and placed on the lower site, or about six hundred feet above the wharf above mentioned would serve to retain the ice in French Basin and the upper reaches of the river and keep the vessel berths in Annapolis free and safe.
Under date of Jan. 14, 1907, Mr. Hodwell, resident engineer at Halifax, reports that there is a probability that the Annapolis Iron Mining Company may at an early date either establish a smelter at Annapolis or may thenco ship their ore by water; and if this project materializes, it will emphasize the need for such improvement of existing shipping facilities as will be afforded by the projected ice barrier. He therefore strongly recommends that an appropriation of $75,000 to $100,000 be made as soon as possible.
There is the report of an experienced engineer who has examined the harbour in the winter season and has seen the action of these ice floes, and who is of opinion that the building of these piers will operate as a barrier to retain the ice. It may be that when these piers are completed, it will be possible to place a superstructure of a steel bridge upon them. If that should be the case, I do not myself see that there would be any public objection to it being done: but of course I would not propose to parliament the construction of these piers for the purpose of utilizing them for a bridge. As I understand the report of the engineer, the reason parliament voted the money for this
work some two or three years ago, before I became minister, was because it would be useful for the purposes of shipping, as making the Annapolis harbour safe. " The Annapolis valley is perhaps the richest section of the whole province of Nova Scotia, It is rich in agricultural products, and is a great fruit district. Large shipments of apples are made from Annapolis to the old country; and if the harbour is made safe, vessels will resort there in a much larger number than at present, and it will become an important shipping point in the winter. I am told that there are also in the vicinity large deposits of valuable iron ore, which will probably be shipped ^at Annapolis if these improvements are made. We can all realize the enormous advantage of having a port open in the winter season as well as in the summer, and if for this comparatively small expense Annapolis harbour can be placed in that position, I feel that the money will be very well expended.

I do not know whether I can make the matter any plainer than the minister has done, but I would like to offer an explanation. Annapolis Basin is an arm of the Bay of Fundy and is open during the winter season. Ice does not form on the basin or the harbour. The Annapolis river flows into this basin.
Is the port of Digby open all the year round?

Yes. It is on another arm of the same basin. The Anna polis river flows from the basin into the bay some twenty miles. The fall of the tide on this river and in the basin is 28 feet. The ice forms during the winter, very heavily up this river to the town of Bridgetown, some 20 miles, and with a fall of 28 feet it will naturally float down during the fall of the tide and go into the Annapolis harbour. After it proceeds down a certain distance, it returns with the incoming tide again. While this ice flows in and out, it does immense damage to the wharfs and shipping, so that in the end the harbour is rendered useless for shipping purposes during the winter simply because of the floating in and out of the ice floes. The purpose of these piers is to prevent, not the formation of ice in the river, but its floating down at falling tide into the Annapolis harbour; and if that purpose be accomplished Annapolis would be made a winter shipping port.
Are these piers to be built all the way across the estuary of the Annapolis from the south to the north shore.
At present it is only proposed to build three piers; but later on, if tliG experiment proves successful, several more piers will be built, which will extern} across the river.
Are they to be equidistant the one from the other?
No.
With regard to the firm of Reid and Archibald, how is it they were not made to carry out their contract? I presume they saw the specifications before tendering.
They refused to sign the contract, and you cannot compel a party who has tendered to sign a contract. All you can do is to make him forfeit his deposit, which was done in this case.

There are times when it is a hardship to make a party tendering forfeit his deposit. I am not referring to this particular instance, but to another case which was one of great hardship. The party tendering acted in good faith, but found afterwards that the plans were so drawn up that the risk was greater than he anticipated. Of course, he saw the plans and specifications before putting in his tender, but the time was short and he had not the opportunity to make as careful an examination as he should have done. But when he found afterwards, after more careful investigation, that the work was more difficult than appeared at first sight, lie declined to enter into a contract and his deposit was forfeited. It seems to me that when, owing to circumstances over which he can have no control, a party who tenders refuses to execute a contract, and has acted in good faith in tendering, his deposit should be returned. That may be a dangerous principle to act upon, but when there is absolute good faith and no suspicion of collusion, I think the deposit should be refunded. The government lias no right to take a man's money for nothing.
What is the object of the piers across the Annapolis? Is it to prevent the ice going down into the harbour?
Yes.

We have in the province of Quebec an old saying, always found to be true, and that is that you cannot possibly resist the movement of the ice. You may impede it to a certain extent by building piers, but nothing will prevent the ice making its way eventually.
Would the flow of the tide be as great in the rivers you have in mind. In the Annapolis river" there is no water left after a short time and the ice would go to the bottom.

The rivers I particularly refer to have no tide. But it is a saying with us that no strength of piers will keep the ice back from its course. If these piers are intended to stop the ice, the money will be wasted. We have had experience Mr. PUGSLEY.
of that for years in the vicinity of Three Rivers. You can impede the ice to a certain extent but you cannot prevent its following its natural course. But to block the ice and prevent it flowing out seems an impossibility.

We have a practical demonstration of it. When the river was frozen over, the conditions happened to be very favourable, there was a wind from the west and it was snowing. The ice caught and froze clear across, and remained for about five weeks, no ice moving in the river at all. The harbour below was absolutely free, and, as I said, a vessel came in and loaded from the ice.
The idea of this is to delay the ice there at low tide?
Or at any time. If the ice is formed, it will remain there-a solid mass of ice.
I understand, the minister is now asking for new tenders. Will the contractors be required to supply all the material for the work?
All except the creosoted timber. That is furnished by the department.
I understand the hon. member (Mr. Pickup) to say that there are about 125 or 135 vessels at this harbour.
Upwards of 200.
Is this the place that is called 'Annapolis Royal'? For I do not see any other.
Yes.

I have here the trade and navigation returns, and I find that in the year ending March 31 last, the arrivals were 19 British vessels, with a tonnage of 5,462, and six foreign vessels with a tonnage of 1,160, or 25 in all, with a tonnage of 6,622, instead of 145 vessels as mentioned by the hon. member. The outgoing vessels numbered 36 British, with a tonnage of 8,906 and 10 foreign with a tonnage of 3,245 or 46 in all, with a tonnage of 12,151 tons-a wonderful difference between these returns and the statement that has been made. If, during the whole season of navigation, and that is the season-I assume, during which the greater share of the produce would be shipped, the apples for instance-there is only this number of vessels, the place is hardly of the importance one would be led to suppose from the figures that have been given. It may be that, if they could continue navigation winter and summer, more might be done, but the figures do not indicate that this is a port of very much importance. I do not know on what the hon. gentleman bases his statement of the number of vessels.

Last year on account of the lumber trade being bad, there were not so many vessels entering and clearing. I referred to two years previous. The coastwise vessels are not included in those returns, I am sure.
Though the coastwise vessels, no doubt, are small, I should think the returns would include them.
What is the width of the whole estuary or river along which these piers are to be built
About 1,800 feet.
Then, the piers will be 180 feet apart?
On the average.

Is it the intention to have chains from pier to pier to prevent the ice going down through the openings?
there any certainty of either ? Is it not the way of prudence to wait until there is something tangible in the way of development and business ? The thing would he different if you could show that a large iron deposit was being worked and a smelting business established. But you do not show that, but only a possibility. But there is one certainty, and that is that you are putting in your money, and that without any official indication of great present trade or strong possibility of trade for the future. After all, what goes out of Annapolis is largely a local traffic. The apples for export, I believe, largely go by another way. The apples for St. John and the provinces may cross the bay. But I think that most of this trade is done before this ice trouble commences. As I understand it, this ice trouble develops mainly in the spring.
All winter.
No.

You have a space of sixty yards between your piers, and you have a fall of twenty-eight feet of tide. When that tide is running out, it must have considerable force. Any ice in that tide must go out like the very mischief, and surely will be carried out through a space sixty yards wide.
The ice is in such large cakes that coming down it would block. That is proved by experience. The result would be an ice bridge behind the piers and a clear harbour below.

It may be that the ice will be in sufficiently large cakes to catch on the piers and prevent any going through. But when the tide is cavorting around and breaking up ice, it generally succeeds in getting into smaller pieces than that would indicate. And I should be very much afraid to bring up a small vessel at the moment when this pernickety ice might take it into its head to come down on that twenty-eight-foot tide and play the mischief with the boat. Now, in reference to the number of vessels in the harbour, there is a general statement made here of 245 vessels. But the customs officer, whose business it is to keep the records, finds-as has been shown by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule)-only 46 vessels. That is a great disparity. If there is such an awful falling off within two or three years, does not the minister think he ought to be cautious and wait to see whether the rest^ of the shipping goes away also ? I would like the committee to notice that there is an expenditure of $160,000 or $170,000, made, apparently, on an airy saying that there are iron ores somewhat near, and that there is just a possibility that these may be exported. There is another^ bare possibility that a smelter may be built there. But is

There would not be any rouble with ice up to December, I sup-iose- that is, the summer and fall navigation is free of that difficulty. There is mother point:	I understand the minister
;o say that the engineer, Mr. Dodwell, had recommended the appropriation of the noney for this purpose. It struck me at the time that it is not quite within the sphere if an engineer to recommend public appropriations. The engineer is the arm upon which the executive authority rests, the minister and his colleagues are to be the judges of appropriations. The appropriations are made presumably upon advisable or necessary grounds, but generally commercial grounds are those that weigli. When the minister or'the government come to the conclusion that for commercial reasons an expenditure of money is advisable, then the engineer comes m with advice as to the best plan to adopt, what form of construction will be most suitable, &c it does not seem to me that it is the .duty of the engineer of a minister to advise appropriation" here or there. If he finds a work in need of repair or something of that kind he may advise appropriations, but ne should hardly advise for or against a work except on scientific grounds.

My hon. friend, I think, is hardly right. The engineer should not give advice as to the commercial advantage of any particular work unless he is asked for such advice, but m my own experience as minister I very often ind properly rely upon the opinion of the resident engineer as to the necessity for any particular work. For receive a petition asking for the cons r -tion of a wharf or urging that some dredging should be done. I very often send a memorandum to the chief engineer asking vim to instruct the resident engineer to report as to the necessity for and the cost

proposed work. In that case it will De tne duty of the engineer to look carefully into the business done at the particular place, to examine the proximity of the proposed wharf to some other wharf or to other harbours. In the case of a breakwater we may ask him to report how far it is from the next harbour of refuge or the next shipping port and generally to report as to the necessity for constructing the work at the particular place indicated In this particular case, suppose that the petition was presented to the minister for this particular work supported by the member for the district and by Mr. Corbett, a gentleman engaged in business in Annapolis since the eighties, and by other +i?-Slnfss men>
if the minister had referred this to the chief engineer and had asked mm to have a careful inquiry made by the resident engineer as to the necessity for and the advantage of the proposed work and its probable cost, I would think in that case it would he quite proper for the engineer to take into consideration all the circumstances connected with this proposed work; to consider its advisability its practicability,-

Comparing the explanations of the minister on this matter last year and to-day I think we have a right to be suspicious that this has something to do with a municinal bridge as mentioned by my hon. friend from Montreal.
I am aware that the gentleman representing the county is well informed in connection with this case; he has so stated last vear and this afternoon as well. Is there any suggestion that these piers will ultimately be used for a municipal bridge or a provincial bridge?
Not that I have any knowledge of, no, sir.
Would it be possible to put a superstructure of steel or iron over these piers that would transform them into a provincial or municipal bridge?

That is a question which has not been looked into at all.
It has not been brought to my notice I directly or indirectly.
Will the minister say he will not allow the piers to be used in future as a municipal bridge without the consent of parliament?

If my hon. friend means that I would not be a consenting party to contributing any moneys of my department for the purpose of erecting a superstructure upon these piers, I will certainly give him and the committee that assurance.
I have learned long since that is the time to bid a certain gentleman good morning when you meet him.

Especially when you meet him often.
Mr-BLAIN. I may say to my hon. friend that this will not hurry along his case.
I cannot help it.

I think this is a fair request I think we have every right to be suspicious that this is for a purpose that my hon. friend is unwilling to reveal to the committee and I think it is only fair that my hon. friend should pledge his word that he will not allow this work, either now or in the future, to be used for any municipal *).r Provincial bridge. Every man knows that it is a strange procedure to build piers m the river to keep the ice back in order to prevent it from interfering with the harbour. Everybody knows that it must he experi-

mental in the main. It is rumoured-indeed the gentleman sitting beside me says it is current in that section of the province-that this is to be used for a municipal or provincial bridge. Before we consent to vote the item finally it is quite fair for the minister to promise the committee that he will not allow the provincial government or any municipality to put a superstructure upon these piers without the consent of parliament.
The minister would have no authority to do it.

Will my hon. friend (Mr. A.
K. Maclean) state that he is not aware that some such suggestion has been contemplated and discussed in that section of Nova Scotia?
I cannot say.
My hon. friend does not want to say.

If the hon. gentleman wants an answer all I can say is that I have never heard of such a suggestion in my life. Of course, it may be true. I am not saying that it is not, but I live quite a distance from the locality and I do not know it. What I said was that the minister would have no authority to grant permission to the provincial government or to a municipality to put a superstructure upon these piers.

The government of which my hon. friend is a prominent supporter has done it before. I had the duty myself of bringing to the attention of this House a case down in the county of Richmond and Wolfe. We had an estimate placed before this House to build a wharf in the town of Disraeli and for two years in succession the item pased the House with the explanation from the minister that it was for a wharf. Evidence was produced on the floor of this House that no vessel carrying freight ever entered that harbour and at this moment upon these piers that were constructed for a wharf, there is a municipal bridge and the old municipal bridge has been removed. Yet the government will not say that they have no intention of doing any such thing again.
Does the hon. gentleman say that evidence has been produced that no vessel has stopped at that wharf?

Yes. I visited the town and produced on the floor of this House, in the presence of the minister's predecessor, a sworn statement from a gentleman who had lived there for twenty-five years, and was a former mayor, that at no time in the history of the town had there ever been a vessel of any description carrying produce into that wharf.
Was that before or after the wharf was built? How does the hon. gentleman expect a vessel to go to a wharf until after it is built?
There was no vessel to go there.
My information is that vessels did go there before and that they have gone there since the wharf was built.

I may say to my hon. friend that it is absolutely impossible for a vessel of any description to go underneath the bridge, to enter the wharf which public money has been expended to build. My hon. friend must know that if he knows anything about his department.
It happens in that case that vessels land and deliver their cargo on the lower side of the bridge and at the wharf which is at the lower side of the bridge.
My hon. friend has not been there.
That is my information.

I have been there. That is another impossibility because there is a superstructure of a railway along the other side of the bridge that makes it absolutely impossible for a vessel seven feet high to go into the wharf. I would ask my hon. friend to produce to the committee this afternoon a report showing how many vessels have entered there.

We were discussing the question as to whether or not this vote to provide for the erection of ice piers should be passed. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) did dilate upon some alleged or imaginary wrong that occurred somewhere in Quebec a couple of years ago in reference to the D'Israeli bridge, but my hon. friend need not harp back to ancient history or dig up from the archives anything that gave him satisfaction at that time in order to enable this committee to consider what they should do about this particular vote. My hon. friend's soul seems to have been somewhat vexed as to the question of the possibility of a municipal bridge being erected over these piers. As a matter of fact, in the province of Nova Scotia, the erection of bridges is entirely in the hands of the provincial government. There is therefore no possibility of a municipal bridge which he seems to regard as being a frightful iniquity that might be perpetrated upon somebody-I do not know whom. There is no danger of that occurring in Nova Scotia. With regard to the question as to whether or not the object of the erection of these piers is for the purpose of having a bridge ultimately built, I may say that in so far as hon. gentlemen

supporting the government from Nova Scotia are concerned, we have not heard of there being any such proposition involved in this vote. I may say further that I have learned of the case that was put forth in regard to this matter by Mr. Geo. E. Corbett, who was the Conseravtive candidate in the county of Annapolis in the election of last autumn. Mr. Corbett claimed in the county last year a great deal of credit from the people there because he had come to Ottawa and impressed upon the government the necessity of undertaking this work, and he said that he and not Mr. Pickup, the representative of the county, was the gentleman who ought to receive all the credit that the county could give on account of it. My hon. friend ought to be fair and frank about this thing. We are fair and frank about it. I may say that if as a result of the erection of these piers in the Annapolis harbour the provincial government should come to this government and say that this is a public work that can be utilized for two purposes I do not see any reason why the department should not consider it because I do not see who is going to be hurt by it. If we have the navigation of Annapolis harbour improved by the erection of these piers, is it going to hurt any body if the_ provincial government should say: We will be able to secure a highway here by making an arrangement satisfactory to both governments? That would be no great iniquity. There is no necessity of the hon. gentleman holding up his hands in holy horror at such a proposition.
You have your hands up now.

Well I am only suggesting that my hon. friend need not get into the same attitude. As far as I am concerned and as far as every other hon. gentleman supporting the government from Nova Scotia is concerned, we have not heard of this bridge project, and I see no reason why the two governments should not treat on the subject.

I am sure the committee is highly pleased with the lucid explanation given by my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) as to why this money should be voted. But did you notice that he let the cat out of the bag when he said that at some future time he would not object to see erected on these piers a superstructure for a municipal or provincial bridge. '
You might also notice that I said I had never heard of such a proposition.

But the hon. gentleman seemed to have it in his mind that such a thing is quite possible, and if it is not going to^ be done there is nothing to prevent the minister pledging his word now that the piers will not be used for such a purpose.

In Ontario, the municipalities construct their oyvn bridges and it is a question of considerable importance to know whether it is the policy of this government to construct ice piers which may afterwards be used for municipal or provincial bridges. We all know very well that when the appropriation was made for the D'Israeli wharf it was pointed out that there was no water in the lake to enable boats to get to it and no boats in the lake, engaged in commercial venture to use the wharf when built. It was pointed out that the D'lsraeli wharf would simply be a municipal bridge and it is to-day a municipal bridge and the only one in the municipality. Will the minister pledge his word to the committee that these piers shall not in future be used for the purpose of a municipal bridge?

I thought the question of the D'Israeli wharf was settled some years ago. If my hon. friend from Peel thinks it_ is not settled I would ask him to consult with Mr. Champoux, the late Conservative candidate in Bichmond and Wolfe at the last election and with whom my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) acted as a detective on one oc casion.
I will ask the Chairman if it is in order to call a member of this House a detective?

I will withdraw that. At all events the member for Peel went down to Richmond and Wolfe some years ago to investigate the D'Israeli wharf and he met there Mr. Champoux a disappointed contractor who wanted to sell some lumber to the Public Works Department, and he got from Mr. Champoux certain information. Now, Mr. Champoux was the Conservative candidate in Richmond and Wolfe last election and he conducted his campaign in D'Israeli where this wharf was constructed but he did not mention the wharf and he did not make any charge against the government in connection therewith. True, the government built a wharf at the mouth of Black creek which empties into Lake Aylmer and later on the municipality filled up a part of that creek and they now cross on it, but it is not correct to say that the government ever built a bridge" for that municipality.
They built half of it.

If my hon. friend from Peei wants to go down on another picnic to Richmond and Wolfe he will find there is no obstruction from the railway bridge and that Mr. Champoux will tell him that he did not make any complaint about the D'Israeli wharf when he appealed to the electors last fall. I may tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) that Lake Aylmer is no small stream; it is 13 or 14 miles long and 4 or 5 miles broad and there are boats plying on the lake, and if they are not do-

ing a freight business, surely the people who live in Stratford, D'lsraeli, Lake Weed-on, Garthby and other towns on the lake have a right to have their share of public expenditure. I have a petition from the people of the township of Stratford asking for a wharf at Stratford, and these people know the needs of the locality. 1 have forwarded that petition to the Minister of Public Works and if he does not grant the prayer of the petition this year I trust he will place a vote in the estimates for it next year.
Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tobin) regard the D'lsraeli wharf as a municipal bridge?
I do not.
Part of D'Israeli is situated on one side of that water and part on the other, and the only way to get across is by that bridge or wharf on which this government spent $7,500.
The hon. gentleman knows very well that the government never appropriated any money to build a bridge at D'Israeli.
That's right enough; they called it a wharf.

May I suggest that we should take a business view of the situation. In this case, where the work is to be for the joint benefit of the Dominion and of the province it would seem as though both should mutually subscribe for that work. If I should build a hoiioC on a vacant lot and a neighbour comes later on and builds next to me he has to pay me for the use of my mitoyen wall as soon as he takes advantage of it. I do not know any reason, if these ice piers are needed to stop the ice and are constructed for that purpose and succeed in standing the pressure of the ice, and are properly located, why thev should not eventually be used for a bridge; but the moment the provincial authorities ask for the right to use them for a bridge, they ought to contribute their fair share of the expense; and all we ask of the minister is that he will give us some assurance that in such a case an adequate compensation will be demanded.

A somewhat similar question came up not very long ago in regard to some ice piers which had been built for the protection of the banks of a river and also for the benefit of navigation in another province. The municipality in which they were constructed proposed to utilize them, with the consent of the government, for the placing upon them of a steel superstructure to be used in place of a bridge which had either been carried away by freshets or had decayed. I stated that in my opinion the local authorities should be
permitted to utilize those piers for that purpose on condition that they would be willing to enter into an engagement with my department that they would keep those piers in repair for all time, free of expense to the federal government. I do not see what objection there could be from the standpoint of the public interest to an arrangement of that character. With regard to the wharf at D'Israeli, I am surprised that my hon. triend from Peel (Mr. Blam) should allow himself to be misled as to the facts of the case. When he went there on the occasion to which he has referred, he must have studiously avoided the side of the wharf which is frequented by vessels navigating the lake. The same rather unjustifiable and inconsiderate statement was made at the last session of parliament. A report has been made by the resident engineer to the effect that the vessels do go to that wharf and that it is a very useful structure for the purposes of navigation. It is true, the wharf having been built, the municipal authorities use one end of it for supporting a bridge, and their doing so does not interefere with the purposes for which it was built. I hope my hon. friend will get more reliable information before he again speaks on that subject in this House. With regard to the usefulness of these piers, I cannot say what the minister will do in the future, but if application should be made on the part of the provincial government for permission to use these piers to bear the superstructure of a bridge, all I can say is that if I happened to be the Minister of Public Works at that time,
I would insist that before that permission should be given, an arrangement for adequate compensation should be entered into -it might take the form of a money payment or the form of an engagement on the part of the provincial authorities to keep the piers in repair, whichever would be best in the public interest. Whatever conclusion would be arrived at would depend on the circumstances. What I want to assure the House is that, so far as my information goes, these piers are being built for the purposes of navigation. These are the sole purposes put forward in the report of the engineer. The engineer is very strongly of opinion that the piers will prove beneficial, that they will form a solid ice bridge or jam at the head of the Annapolis harbour, and thus make the harbour reasonably free from ice and otherwise safe in the winter season.

As my hon. friend has introduced the subject of the Disraeli wharf, I suppose we shall be allowed to make an answer. In doing so, it will be necessary to take up a little of the time of the committee.
