I wish to draw attention to a matter of great importance with regard to the Sissiboo or Weymouth river in the county of Digby. This river is crossed by a bridge of the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company some distance below the town of Weymouth. The Sissiboo river is one of the principal waterways of western Nova Scotia and of much importance the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company, as I am credibly informed, purposes during the coming summer to rebuild the bridge, and it is said that it will be constructed with a span of some 35 or 40 feet I may be permitted to refer very briefly to the history of this bridge. In 1877-8 the Western Counties Railway was projected through Digby county designed to cross the river at this point. The business of the town of Weymouth was then chiefly done two and a half miles down the river below the location of the present business centre. The people of that neighbourhood were so anxious to secure railway connection that they purchased the right of way and practically built a new town two and a half miles more up the river where the railway crosses it. At that time the plans which were approved by the Department of Public Works required a draw or span of 40 feet in width. When the bridge was built however the railway company reduced this span giving only 35 feet in the clear. Ever since this bridge was constructed, the people have been under great disadvantage with regard to shipping facilities, owing to this narrow draw. The Dominion Atlantic Railway Company is as stated proposing to rebuild the bridge, and I am informed have a structure already prepared and on the ground-for the erection of a bridge giving no more than 35 feet in the clear. When the business interests of Weymouth and the outside shipping interests were advised of this, they entered a protest, and the building of the bridge was deferred until that protest was settled. I am informed that an application was made in 1807 to the Board of Railway Commissioners for the reconstruction of the bridge with a 35 feet draw, and that permission was given by the commission but that subsequently it was found the_ railway company had not submitted their plans to the Department of Public Works, and the wrok on the bridge was completely suspended owing to this agitation of the shipping and local interests. The trade of Weymouth is of considerable importance, a large lumber business is done there, a large pulp industry is carried on, and as time goes

on the port will become still more important from a commercial point of view than it is now. The people and the shipping interests of that district are extremely anxious that a draw' or span of 60 feet in width should be placed in the neighbourhood. It is not only the interests of the town of Weymouth but the interests of shipping generally which would be benefited by that wider span. The railway company has.
I understand, having been informed of this demand for a wider draw, considered it would be a hardship to impose on them the total cost of its construction. As regards the necessity for a wider draw, I am informed that the carrying of lumber to-day is done in vessels of greater beam than 15 or 25 years ago, and that consequently a vessel	of practically the same tonnage
would require to-day a wider passage than fifteen or twenty-five years ago. I am informed by shippers that they are now obliged to charter old vessels simply because the cannot get a modern vessel to go through the present draw, and that is one reason why they urge that a wider draw should be built. Further, they have to transport a large quantity of lumber down below this bridge in barges or scows or by teams, which imposes an additional cost amounting to fifty cents per 1,000 feet.
The railway company is suggesting, 1 believe, that the government should assist in the payment of the cost of construction of this wider draw. With reference to that feature, I would quote from 'Hansard.' volume IV., of 1906, page 7052, etc. Under the item of expenditure on harbours and rivers in British Columbia, I find this rfe ference.

There is one new item there:
Pitt river

substitution of a 230-foot through truss for original 132-foot truss of draw-span on C.P.R. bridge, inclusive of accessory works, $55,085.
He goes on to say :
The Canadian Pacific Railway built a bridge across the river there a number of years ago. They got the permission of the Department of Public Works to build this bridge. The Canadian Pacific Railway are renewing the bridge; they were building a new bridge last year, and it was then found necessary in the interests of navigation to widen the span. We asked them to do so, and they took the ground that having received permission to build according to their original plans, the government should pay for any widening of the spans the Justice Department gave its decision that under the circumstances the government should be liable. Therefore, we were in the position of having either to accept the old span or to pay our share of the cost. This is the amount found by the engineers to be due to the Canadian Pacific Railway by the government.
I ask and urge that what the government did in the case of the Pitt River bridge in British Columbia, in 1906; they should do at the present time in the case of the Sis-siboo or Weymouth bridge, and in any case a span of sixty feet should be required to be built. Some time ago, I had the privilege of discussing this matter with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-ley), and he told me that it would receive most careful consideration. I merely present these facts to-day in order that the claims of that district may be fully recognized and not overlooked. I trust the application of the people of Weymouth for a sixty foot draw may meet the favourable consideration of the Department of Public Works and the government, and that, if the government is going to pay any part of this and not require the railway to bear all the cost, provision will be made in the estimates during the present session.

The matter presented by mv hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) is not new, either as to the bridge at Weymouth or the action taken by parliament in 1906. If my hon. friend read the papers which I placed at his disposal-as I have no doubt he did -he found the matter referred to there. The position is this: About a year ago, when the Dominion Atlantic Railway were about to rebuild their bridge at this point, my attention was called to the matter by the late hon. member for Digby, Mr. Copp. At his urgent solicitation, I notified the company that they must not proceed with the building of the bridge upon the proposed plan, for the reason that they had not followed the old order in council passed some thirty years ago, which provided that they should build a bridge with a span of not less than 40 feet, whereas they had built with a span of 34 feet, 8 inches. It is contended now, on behalf of the company, that they would have the right to rebuild the bridge according to the design approved of in 1878, and they argue that if the government, in the interests of navigation and for the benefit of the people of Weymouth, should require them to build a bridge with a span, say, 55 or 60 feet, the government should do as they did in the case of the Pitt River bridge, pay part of the cost. The matter is under consideration, but I am not prepared to say what action will be taken in regard to it.
Carried.

I do not intend that any undue haste in calling votes ' Carried ' shall prevent me from saying a word on this subject. I have had experience here of being prevented from saying something by the extreme application of rules, but I do not propose at this time of my life to be so very easily turned down. I have no objection to the passing of this item. I wish to speak of the unnecessary alarm that

appears to be felt on the part of some hon. members on the opposition side concerning the use that may be made of these piers. If these hon. gentlemen understood the bridge law of the province of Nova Scotia, they would not have the notions about these piers that they have. I dare say it is thought that it would be popular in the county of Annapolis for a representative to be able to get this bridge out of the Dominion money. Let me tell these hon. gentlemen that such a thing is not thought of. He would not make one vote, and he would not detain a gentleman on the road for five minutes by trying to entertain him with such a story as that he was going to build this bridge. I think the mistake arises from our hon. friends from Ontario applying in the case of Nova Scotia the Ontario law respecting bridges and roads. I admire the public spirit of the people of Ontario and the way they have maintained their own roads and bridges direct out of their own pockets. Such is not the custom or law of Nova Scotia, nor has it ever been. Ever since Nova Scotia first became a province, its roads and bridges have been built and maintained out of public government money. There is no such thing as a tax upon the people for building bridges or maintaining roads. Up to 1883, the tax payers did not contribute a cent either directly or indirectly towards the maintenance of roads or bridges. In that year, there was passed what is known as the Bridge Act, under which the government of the province was empowered to borrow money to build large steel bridges wherever they were needed in the province, the interest on that money to be paid, not directly by the individuals who enjoyed the privilege of the bridge, but out of the road grant. That is:	There is a road grant paid by
the government to each county out of the revenue of the province-not out of direct taxation, and from this allowance, the government deducted enough to cover the interest on the sums spent in building bridges within the county. The only effect that the building of a bridge had upon the individual in the county would be that there would not be so large a road grant that year as if there had been no interest on the money invested in the bridge to be deducted. But, for the last two years, even this has been done away with, and the counties do not pay anything toward the interest on the bridges-the provincial government pays both principal and interest. Therefore, my hon. friends will understand that the people of Annapolis are not concerned about the building of these piers or that bridge. If a bridge is required at Annapolis, it will be built by the government of Nova Scotia.
I submit to my hon. friends that from one end of the province of Nova Scotia to the other, they cannot point to any case in which the government of Nova Scotia ever Mr. d. d. McKenzie.
called upon the Dominion government to contribute a single farthing toward the building or maintaining of a work that legitimately belonged to the provincial government. By no subterfuge, plan or scheme has the provincial government tried to cause the Dominion government to undertake any duty or face any expenditure that properly belonged to the local authority. They are well able to look after their own affairs and I assure hon. gentlemen they are not asking any favours from this government or asking this government to do anything which is the duty of the local government or themselves to perform. Some hon. gentlemen may not understand how these expenditures in our province bear upon the individual. The spending of this money by this government would not relieve the farmers or merchants of that district of any expense as this work would be done by the provincial government and not by the municipality. It is not felt at all by the individual. I do not understand the alarm of members of the opposition even if such an expenditure was to be made in Nova Scotia. Only last night it was suggested that the government should build a bridge and a piece of road in Kingston. That was considered a first rate proposition, at all events there was no opposition to it.
That was a proposition to construct and maintain a road in front of property purchased by the Minister of Militia.

That does not make the slightest difference. We have in Halifax more government and imperial property than there is in Kingston, yet we never heard of either the imperial or Canadian government contributing one farthing towards the maintenance of anything municipal in connection with that city simply because that property was there. I think that rule should appiy at Kingston as well as at* Halifax. An hon. member from Manitoba had a bridge of this kind built in his country, but the opposition raised no objection to it and it was even suggested that this government should paint it and maintain the approaches. This was regarded by these gentlemen as all right because it came from one of themselves. I do not think it is right, I think that each government should confine its activity to the sphere allotted to it by the constitution.
I simply wanted to point out that there was no object in any Nova Scotia member urging this government to build a work of this kind for municipal purposes as it would not relieve the people of the neighbourhood. The farmers and the people generally of Nova Scotia are not concerned as to where the money comes from.

It is extremely interesting to have the hon. member for Victoria County, Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) tell

us that the people of Nova Scotia do not wish any money spent upon anything provincial, tell us that this sort of thing may be done in other provinces but in Nova Scotia it is never done. The hon. member's predecessor succeeded in persuading the minister to spend a considerable sum of money 11 miles up Middle river in his own county in order to build sheer dams to protect the land of farmers on that river, and also to spend a considerable sum on the Baddeck river to protect the farmers. These are small streams, they are absolutely unnavigable and could not possibly come under the head of harbours and rivers. It comes with a strange grace from the hon. member for Victoria county to tell us that the Dominion government is never asked or expected to spend money in Nova Scotia for provincial purposes, when m his own county we have some of the most glaring examnles of the contrary that are to be found in the Dominion of Canada.

Whilst we gather from the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, that in 1883 the ' Greater Bridges Act ' as it was called, was passed in Nova Scotia and that all bridges in that province are supposed to he built by the local government, it is not a new story, in the province of Nova Scotia at election time, that it is an excellent thing to have a good friend at court. We heard it in the local elections in 1901, in Nova Scotia when we were told that by supporting the local government in certain countries we would have a greater possibility than we had before of securing compensation for the building of the eastern extension of the Intercolonial Railway, and while it is a fact that the expense for bridges is to be bc.rne by the government in that province, it must also be borne in mind that the revenue of that province is not great, being slightly more than $1,000,000 a year, so that it will not enable the provincial government to erect many $200,000 bridges in Nova Scotia. I submit that if the electors in Annapolis approached the local government at Halifax and asked them to erect a bridge across this stream at a cost of $200,000 or $250,000, the Nova Scotia government would take into consideration the amount of traffic to be catered to and they would hesitate to spend such a large sum of money.
But I do submit that if a candidate for the local House were to go to the government at Halifax and say:	The estimated
cost of a bridge across this river is $200,-
000.	the estimated cost of the piers is $160,000 or $170,000 the superstructure wall only cost $60,000 or $70,000, and then would add that the federal government at Ottawa had been good enough to undertake to furnish the foundations and piers and all that we would require to do would
i>e to furnish the superstructure, that candidate would have a strong argument to submit to the government at Halifax and would be very likely to succeed in his application. The hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) has pointed out a couple of instances in the county of Victoria where money was spent twelve miles up the Middle river and on Baddeck river, for the protection of the lands of farmers there. In the county of Colchester, during the by-election of 1907, a sum of money was spent at Tatamagouche for the purpose of erecting a wharf and when the hon. member for Colchester put a question on the Order Paper in this House asking to know* what the depth of water was at that wharf he was told that there was no water at low tide and that there were four feet of water at high tide. The hon. member for Colchester has been exhibiting a photograph in this House. I do not know whether he is here to-day or not, but he exhibited this photograph to a large number of members and it shows that this so-called wharf is nothing more or less than a bridge. It shows a horse and cart and some people on the bridge and if you look at the ordinary high water mark along the shore, as shown in the photograph, you will see that it would have to be a high spring or fall tide that would give four feet of water. It is a dangerous precedent to establish in this House that any of the municipalities or provinces can look to the federal government for assistance in constructing bridges. It is but entering the thin edge of the wedge, and if it becomes known that upon the pretense of having ice breakers erected in one constituency and if these ice breakers can afterwards be used for the purpose of erecting a bridge, I have no doubt, that all kinds of suggestions and petitions will come to this government asking for ice piers, where, as a matter of fact, it is a bridge that is desired rather than ice breakers. It may be called a wharf in the petition or in the estimates, it may be called ice breakers in the petition or the estimates, but I submit that where it is a bridge that is reallv sought, that makes a great deal of difference. A rose by any other name would smell as sweet. There was a statement made by the Minister of Public Works with regard to the traffic to be served at this point. I take it to be correct as stated by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that they have a rise and fall of the tide there of twenty-eight feet and having the rise and fall of the tide there, as in all other places, twice in twenty-four hours, and the temperature not being of such a character as to allow the formation of large bodies of ice. I would conclude that the interference with shipping caused by these conditions is unimportant. The public

reports indicate that there is a very small number of vessels entering or leaving that port. As far as the shipping of iron ore from that port is concerned, I would like to refer the Minister of Public Works to the fact that in the Mines report, which came to hand this session, the statement is made that the iron mines at Thorbrooke, in Annapolis, employ some 104 men. Their total output of ore is about 300 tons per day and this output is now sent to Londonderry. The report says:
The output now sent to Londonderry is handled by the Dominion Atlantic Kailway Company, whose branch line of 6 miles connects with the mines, and the Intercolonial Railway.

If it is going to be a part of the policy of this government to grant assistance to municipalities and provincial governments in their road-making schemes we should know it. I do not know but that perhaps it might be a commendable policy. I am not committed one way or another with regard to it but I do submit that it might be more profitable to spend the money along such commendable lines rather than to squander it as has been done in the past. But if it is the policy of this government to grant assistance to provincial governments for the purpose of building municipal or provincial bridges it should come before this House clothed properly and bear on its face what it really is. If the purpose is to build a bridge across a river in Nova Scotia or in any other province the application should come before the government in the shape of a petition for a bridge across such river, and it should not come in the guise of an application for an ice pier or a wharf. I do not happen to have the length here because the appropriation was made two years ago, and the details were then given. We are building three at present.
Mr. SPROULE I would like to have the height, the length, and the width of these piers. What is supposed to be the life of this creosoted timber?
So far it has given satisfaction and its use is becoming more general in recent years. I do not know that we have experience enough to say what the life of creosoted timber is.

It seems to me it would be worth while ascertaining whether it would not be the part of wisdom, depending of course on the relative cost and permanency of other materials, to use cement and stone where the teredo worm has to be guarded against.
In some cases we build entirely of concrete, but in this case we are building only the superstructure of concrete. The concrete costs considerably more.

I would like the minister to get me the dimensions of these piers, how much of this work is to be concrete and how much stone, what kind of timber is used, and the quantity for each pier. If we have these details we can estimate the cost.
I will get that information.

Formerly the experiment was tried of covering the piers with copper, and I think it was regarded as a greater preventative against the teredo worm than creosoted timber. When we are spending such large sums of money all these questions should be carefully considered by the minister.
We will give that consideration.
Last year the minister stated that $12,000 worth of timber had been purchased. Was the purchase made by public tender?
No. There are very few dealers in creosoted timber in Canada. The market price was paid.
Was that timber delivered last year?
Yes.
Does the minister think it is in the public interest to purchase $12,000 worth of timber without competition?
Not usually, but this is creosoted timber.
Anybody can creosote.
It is creosoted in the Southern States and there are only two concerns which do that work.
What firm supplied this timber?
The Norfolk Creosoting works.
Is there any correspondence in the Public Works Department from the municipalities of Granville, or Annapolis, or from the local government with respect to this work?
Not since I became a minister, that I have seen.
Prior to that?
I do not know.

According to the trade and navigation returns, there were in Annapolis Royal only eighteen vessels from the United States, one from the British West Indies and one from Norway, carrying an aggregate of 1,679 tons.
There is the coasting trade in addition.

I regret to sec that the estimates for harbours and rivers for Nova Scotia do not contain any sum for contract dredging. Last year contracts were awarded for dredging work in some of the harbours and rivers of Nova Scotia, and I trust that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works may see his way to making provision for the carrying out of those contracts. In my own constituency dredging is most necessary in one or two cases, and I trust that the minister will be able to have an additional vote of $200,000 or $300,000 placed in the supplementary estimates to provide for such cases. I am quite willing that a great many of the usual items under the head of Harbours and Rivers should be abandoned this year; but the matter of dredging is very important, and I think the government and the House generally would agree to a supplementary vote for dredging in several of the provinces.
It has been abandoned in a great many sections in the western part of Canada.

The necessity for dredging may not be so great on the great lakes as it is in the maritime provinces. Another remark I wish to make is that in the province of Nova Scotia at least we have not received from the government dredges the amount of work annually that we might fairly expect. I think that has been the case ever since confederation. The dredges do not get to work early enough in the spring and stop too earlv in the autumn, and the number of hours they work daily is altogether too small. There are a number of places in the province of Nova Scotia where the dredges could easily work all winter. The office in St. John appears to be altogether too inactive and too slow in its supervision of the work. In the province of Nova Scotia we have never obtained the amount of dredging which the necessities of our ports and' harbours demand. Therefore my request is twofold-that we should get more work out of the_ government dredges than we have been doing from confederation down, and that a vote of $200,000 o. $300,000 be placed in the supplementary estimates to carry on dredging in the province of Nova Scotia, for which contracts were entered into in 1908.
Would you get better results from dredging done by the government or by contractors?
I would prefer the work to be done by contractors.

I would like to emphasize the remarks of my hon. friend from Lunenburg. I quite appreciate the neces-1 sity of suspending, for a time at least, all



works that are not absolutely essential; but in the matter of dredging, in some instances where the work has been under contract and has been commenced, I do not observe in the estimates anything for its continuance this year. That may possibly be reasonable in some instances, but in one particular instance of which I am cognizant, the result will be, that if the work is not continued during this season, the work that was done last year will be practically lost to the department. There was some dredging required in Baie Verte, on the border line between Westmoreland and Cumberland. For very many years the municipalities have been asking to have this dredging done, and at the last session of parliament a vote was passed for the purpose, and a contract was entered into, and the work commenced. It was for the purpose of dredging_ a bar which blocked the entrance to the river and the harbour. For some reason this work was suspended in the early autumn, when the bar was only half cut through. If that work is proceeded with this year, and a cutting made through the channel, the work done last season will be available; but if it is allowed to stand and no money provided for the continuance of that contract, the work done last summer will fill in and be practically lost. It seems to me that the minister, in order to save the money already expended should make provision for the continuance of that work. I refer particularly to the dredging of the Port Elgin harbour on the Gaspereau river in the Baie Verte. I would ask the minister to bear this in mind, as it is coupled with the request of my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean). The conditions at Port Elgin are certainly such that the case is much stronger, and I would like to emphasize what has already been said in that regard.
